News.title: Hero neighbour in pyjamas battled house blaze with jet washer before woman tragically died as cops probe murder
News.content:
BLAZE BRAVERY Hero neighbour in pyjamas battled house blaze with jet washer before woman tragically died as cops probe murder

A HERO neighbour in his pyjamas battled a house blaze that killed a woman, as cops probe a suspected murder.

The 48-year-old woman died and eight others were injured in the house fire that tore through a home on Berkley Avenue, Hounslow, West London, just after 1am on Wednesday.



Armed with a jet washer, shopkeeper Satwant Singh, 48, rushed outside to fight the fire while still in his pyjamas.

His daughter had spotted the fire from her bedroom window and woken him up in the middle of the night.



He told The Sun: “I told my wife to get all the children outside and then opened up the alleyway side door and brought the jet wash around the front of the house to spray the fire.

“I could see that the door was on fire but there was smoke everywhere else.



Satwant said he put out “most of the fire”, adding: “I didn’t think about myself, I was just thinking that I needed to help.

“We are Sikhs. My culture says we should help people. It doesn’t matter who you are.”

His wife Barkash, praised his bravery and said she begged him to move from the flames, but that he continued spraying the house.



She said: “He is very brave. I think the water from the jet wash reduced the smoke coming from the house and helped people get out.”

She added: “When we went outside we saw a man who lived in the house on the roof shouting for people to get out.”



Barkash said the fire had calmed down when the fire brigade arrived.

The mum-of-three realised the house next door was on fire when her 14-year-old daughter Jennica rushed into her bedroom.

Jennica said: “I was woken up by a bang and when I looked outside I saw the reflection of fire in the car.”

After the fire, the family couldn’t sleep, Barkash said.

She added: “I can’t forget the sound of people shouting ‘help, help’, neighbours saying to move the vehicles and the man on the roof shouting for people to leave the house. We were so panicked.”



Shaf Akmal, 40, said he was one of the first people outside.

He said: “I saw two men who stood on the back of a car parked in the driveway of the house and broke the downstairs window to pull two people out.”

Shaf’s ring doorbell footage showed the house suddenly being engulfed in flames.

Officers attended the scene alongside the London Fire Brigade and London Ambulance Service.

Nine people were taken to hospital as a result of their injuries, where one woman died.



A murder investigation has since been launched but no arrests have been made so far.

Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, who is leading the investigation, said:

“Our thoughts are first and foremost with the victim’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time, as well as everyone who has been injured.

“Our enquiries are progressing at pace as we work to establish the full circumstances surrounding the fire, which we believe may have been started deliberately.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We understand this to be an isolated incident within a residential address; however, we understand it will cause concern within the local community.”



They urged anyone with information, or footage that may assist the investigation, to contact police.

News.title: British Airways cabin boss ‘sexually assaulted sleeping air hostess at his home after drinking with her at a dinner’
News.content:
BA CREW 'PREYED ON' British Airways cabin boss ‘sexually assaulted sleeping air hostess at his home after drinking with her at a dinner’

A BRITISH Airways cabin boss preyed on a sleeping air hostess after downing beer and wine at his home, a court heard.

Amardip “Amo” Dhariwal, 55, allegedly assaulted the female colleague after boozing with her over dinner.



The ex-lead flight manager is on trial for a single attack on one woman in 2022 — but a jury has heard from two other stewardesses who alleged he raped them on foreign trips.

Dhariwal denies one count of sexual assault by penetration. Reading crown court heard he invited the woman to his then-home in Bracknell, Berks, for dinner, where they drank beer and wine.



The woman, then engaged and now married, said she dozed off as they watched a film and woke to find Dhariwal touching her intimately.

Prosecutor James Partridge told jurors: “They met three months prior to the incident on a flight to Cape Town.



“They got on so well that they met for coffee a few times. She went to his house for taco and movie nights.”

She even referred to Dhariwal as her “work husband”.

Mr Partridge added: “They started watching a film. As they watched it, the victim said she had her legs up.

“She awoke to the defendant touching her.”



He said the woman “felt bewildered” and escaped by finding a key while he was upstairs and called a friend “crying and whispering” on the phone.

Dhariwal, now of Southall, West London, told police: “Anything that happened was consensual.”

The jury was told Dhariwal allegedly raped a colleague in a Singapore hotel room in 2020. She woke naked in his bed, confused by how she got there, she said.

Local police investigated but took no further action and would not help British cops, it was said.

The other stewardess claimed she was assaulted while asleep and drunk in a hotel room in Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur in 2018.



The trial continues.

News.title: Bizarre moment Putin peers at bones of 650-year-old warrior ‘set to be worshipped by Russian soldiers fighting Ukraine’
News.content:
THIS is the bizarre moment Vladimir Putin takes a break from waging war on Ukraine to peer at the bones of a 650-year-old saint.

The ageing dictator has landed on a new tactic to boost morale – sending his soldiers a medieval corpse.



The body of Dmitry Donskoy, who died in 1389, was uncovered during restoration work at Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel.

Famous for fighting the Mongols on the Don river in 1380, the medieval warrior prince was sainted in 1988.



Now Donskoy may enter a warzone once again – with bits of his bones dispatched to the frontline.

Bizarre footage shows the tyrant crossing himself as he bends down to gaze at the desiccated corpse – before lighting a candle in prayer.

The despot rarely visits the frontline – instead cowering in his bunker with more than 800 elite security guards watching his every move.

In the absence of their tyrannical ruler, soldiers will now be able to worship some saintly bones in the midst of deadly drone warfare.

Church official Vakhtang Kipshidze said: “Everyone shares the opinion that the opportunity for such veneration should be provided to Orthodox military personnel as soon as possible.”

Putin has given the plan his go ahead and “best wishes”.



“Even the relics are going to war, but Putin isn’t” taunted Ukrainian news channel Pravda Gerashchenko.

Bits of the skeleton are set to be shipped to the frontline – where some officials believe they can lend “spiritual support”.

The move has also been mocked online, with one commenter posting on X: “Nothing says better about encouraging your troops in a battlefield by parading the corpse of a dead guy.”



Combat wounds can be spotted on his skeleton – though the ruler died of natural causes aged 39.

Just last month, the Russian army lost the bones of Prince Alexander Nevsky.

The relic was being transported for a prayer service against the spiralling fuel crisis.

But the convoy came under attack on the road – and authorities admitted that the shrine had been “completely lost”.

Three Russian soldiers also died in the drone blasts.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Putin does not often visit his ailing armies – and in May was gripped by assassination fears, banning his staff from taking the bus or using mobile phones.

The Russian tyrant, once the world’s ultimate tough guy, went into total meltdown, according to a report from The Financial Times.

News.title: Ukraine diver arrested over Nord Stream pipeline blast nicked while working on set of Hollywood movie starring Sean Penn
News.content:
A UKRAINIAN diver who was arrested over the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline was reportedly detained while working on the set of a Hollywood film about the attack.

Volodymyr Zhuravlyov was arrested in Pula, Croatia on Wednesday on a warrant from Germany.



He is accused of acting alongside a group who planted explosives on the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines near the island of Bornholm in September 2022, German prosecutors have said.

Three of the four pipelines connecting Russia and Germany were blown up in the attack that came just months after Vladimir Putin launched his full scale invasion of Ukraine.



At the time of his arrest, Zhuravlyov was reportedly working as an advisor on a movie about the gas pipeline blasts, starring Adrien Brody and three-time Oscar winner Sean Penn.

He was on the set of Snake Island by US director Doug Liman, Germany’s Legal Tribune Online reported.

Zhuravlyov had already been arrested last year in Poland over the undersea plot.

But the country refused to allow his extradition to neighbouring Germany.

Polish authorities released Zhuravlyov, judging that a Ukrainian attack on the pipelines would have been a legitimate act of war, not a crime.

German investigators think the attack was ordered by the Ukrainian state, aiming to choke off Mad Vlad’s energy exports that could have been used to bolster his war chest.



German prosecutors said Zhuravlyov, who will now be extradited to Germany, “participated in the necessary dives”.

Last year, a Ukrainian suspect identified only as Serhiy Kuznetsov was detained in Misano Adriatrico, near the Italian city of Rimini.

The Ukrainian national has continued to deny having any involvement in the attacks.



Both Nord Stream pipelines were damaged by explosions under the Baltic Sea between Denmark and Sweden.

The blasts caused four leaks as shocking images showed the twisted remains of the pipeline 262ft down in the Baltic Sea.

Around 165ft of pipeline was destroyed or buried under the seafloor.

The attacks sent millions of cubic metres of methane boiling to the sea’s surface and pushed sky-high gas prices even higher – they even caused a mini earthquake.

Kuznetsov and Zhuravlyov are alleged to have used a yacht to sail from the German port of Rostock to the site of the pipelines.



They used fake IDs and intermediaries to get the vessel, prosecutors believe.

The dangerous blasts sparked months of fury over who was behind the attack.

Security experts initially blamed Russian sabotage, as both Ukraine and Poland pointed the finger at Moscow.

Putin had been previously accused of weaponising the energy crisis in a bid to pile pressure on the West.

Russia denied all the allegations at the time, calling them “predictable and stupid”.



Despite the suspects being Ukrainian, officials in Kyiv have also repeatedly denied any role.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said his government knew nothing about any plan to blow up the pipelines.

News.title: Asylum seeker who fled custody after after sex attack on two girls jailed – as victim reveals she tried to end own life
News.content:
BEHIND BARS Asylum seeker who fled custody after after sex attack on two girls jailed – as victim reveals she tried to end own life

A MIGRANT who fled custody after committing sex attacks against two teen girls has been jailed, as one of his victims says she tried to take her own life.

Iranian migrant Pirouz Mofrad, 23, tried to grab two girls, aged 15 and 14, in two different incidents while they were out with their friends.



Mofrad, who entered the UK in 2023 and claimed asylum, was jailed for two years over the sick sex attacks.

In one sickening attack the migrant grabbed a girl at a bus stop and told her he “just wanted to touch her.”



He continued to try and grab her while saying the word “coochie”, a court heard.

He was “staring” at the girl in Southampton, Hampshire, in December 2023 before approaching her at a busy bus stop.



A court was told that the victim’s friend was “sufficiently worried” to move but that Mofrad came over and grabbed the victim’s arm and tried to grab her bottom.

The teen pleaded with Mofrad that she was “too young” but he ignored her while showing her on his own body his breasts and genitals.

The 15-year-old said that after the attack she has “felt anxiety, sadness, anger and fear” and even admitted that she tried to “end her life.”

Mofrad attacked his second victim in the city centre in February 2024.



He approached the 14-year-old while she was with friends and “creeped them out.”

He proceeded to try to grab the 14-year-old while saying words like “coochie” to her and her friends.

The incidents were reported and Mofrad was taken into custody and remanded to HMP Wandsworth with a Sexual Risk Order.

He was then moved to a mental health hospital with a provisional diagnosis of schizophrenia.

He managed to escape the facility on November 5, 2025, and was on the run for a night before being brought back into custody.



His two victims have since told how they are “scared and worried” he will do it again.

Mofrad was convicted by a jury at Lewes Crown Court of escaping from lawful custody on May 1, 2026, he also has two prior convictions of criminal damage.

He has now been sentenced at Southampton Crown Court for two counts of attempted sexual assault after being found guilty following a trial at the same court in July 2026.

The 15-year-old victim read a statement to the court about how the attack affected her.

She said: “The incident has had a substantial and lasting impact on my emotional wellbeing. The effects have stayed with me long after it happened.



“I have found myself thinking about what happened when I don’t want to. I feel like I’m reliving what happened.

“There have been times that I have just wanted it to stop. At my lowest points I have tried to end my life. This is something I never thought I would experience.

“I just wanted to make the pain stop. I have felt anxiety, sadness, anger and fear. It has affected the way I see other people.

“There are times I question myself and wonder if I could have done something differently even though I know it’s not my fault.

“It has affected my relationships and my ability to be around other people.



“It’s hard to explain to people how something happened in the past can affect me in the present.

“What happened took away a part of my sense of safety and peace. I’m still trying to understand how deeply it has affected me. I don’t want it to define me for the rest of my life.”

Judge Nicholas Rowland addressed the victim to assure her: “It’s hard to imagine the amount of courage it has taken, not just to make the report to the police in the first place but to come to these proceedings.

“So when you say you hope it will not define you, you may want to reflect on the courage you have shown in these proceedings and see that it has not defined you – quite the opposite.”

Sentencing the asylum seeker, Judge Rowland continued: “Pirouz Mofrad, I have to sentence you for two offences for attempted sexual assaults of what were then 14 and 15 year old girls.



“These were similar offences against teenage girls who were entitled to feel safe with their friends in the busy city centre and not be accosted by you.

“One was 15 with a friend and it was dark. You were staring at them at the bus stop.

“Her friend was sufficiently worried to move the victim, but you grabbed her arm and then tried to grab her bottom.

“She said she was too young and you said you just wanted to touch her.

“You signalled on your body to your breasts and genitals. You circled them as they waited for the bus.



“The other victim, who was 14, was with friends who were creeped out by your behaviour. You tried to grab her while saying words like ‘coochie’.

“The first victim said she was scared and worried you might do it for others. She felt that way for a year and couldn’t stand close to people.

“She felt sick for months thinking about you. She overdosed shortly after the incident on medication for anxiety and depression.

“Her mother said her mental health had regressed and her school performance severely impacted.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“She has told me in court about the lasting emotional impact this has had on her wellbeing. She has tried to take her life.



“She has experienced anxiety, sadness, anger and fear. She has said to her credit that she did not want this to define her, and I think we can see from these proceedings that they will not.”

If you are affected by any of the issues raised in this article, please call the Samaritans for free on 116123.

News.title: Disturbing details of TikTok star’s final hours before murder revealed – as cops arrest domestic abuser ‘who lured her’
News.content:
A TIKTOK star told family she was going to “end a toxic relationship” hours before she was found dead in a vineyard.

It comes as a convicted domestic abuser with links to the “dark world” of prostitution has been revealed as the prime suspect after Sonia Bellina was murdered in France.



The suspect, who is in his early 30s but who cannot be named for legal reasons, is being held in a secure police station in the south of France following 29-year-old Sonia’s death on or around August 10.

Her battered and naked corpse was found partially burnt in an isolated vineyard in the town of Saint-Gilles, south of Nimes, in the Gard department.



Now, investigators have revealed disturbing new details about Sonia’s last hours – and the man who may have lured her to a horrendously violent attack days before her 30th birthday.

One told The Sun: “The prime suspect is one of two men who were arrested on Wednesday after both were linked to the crime through their mobile phone records, and tracks on their car movements.

“They were in the area where the victim died, and had previous contact with her.

“The main suspect is thought to have carried out the killing, while the second man had a more minor role.

“The prime suspect has convictions for domestic abuse, and other violent crimes.”

Both men are from Nimes, the southern city where Sonia was born and brought up, and where she trained to be a beauty therapist, specialising in eyelash extensions.



Beyond her professional work, Sonia was a hugely popular online influencer, with more than a quarter-of-a-million followers on TikTok, as well as on other mass audience platforms, such as Instagram and Snapchat.

Her regular performances included lip-syncing to old romantic movies, and also pretending to seduce her fans.

An investigating source said: “This may have attracted some very unpleasant people, and the man in custody certainly has a criminal record for abusing women.

“He also allegedly has links to the dark world of prostitution and escort agencies, and may have lured women into this world.”



Prostitution is legal in France but pimping – enticing clients or potential sex workers to pay for sex or accept money for it – is not.

Women involved in the sex industry – whether by choice or coercion – often become the victims of a range of crimes, ranging from murder and rape, to other forms of abuse.

The enquiry into Sonia’s death is currently focused on the theory that a man she knew arranged to meet her, before driving her to the place where she was killed.

There was a five-hour window from the moment Sonia left her family apartment in Nimes and the presumed time of death.



“This has been calculated at shortly after her phone being switched off,” the investigating source added. “Her phone was later found thrown away by the side of the road.”

One family member has told detectives that Sonia set off in the early hours of the morning “to end a toxic relationship” with an unidentified man.

“She left without a bag, saying she would be back within a few hours,” the source said.

“Sonia has only recently met the man, and nobody else in her circle knew him. He was certainly a mystery man.”

Saint-Gilles is a town with a population of 14,000 people, and not a place Sonia is thought to have visited before.



She was taken to a vineyard close to an airfield and a military base before being killed, police believe.

Despite it being so early in the morning, workers were still milling around, but direct witnesses have proved hard to find.

“Nobody heard or saw anything around the presumed time of death,” the insider said. “There are CCTV cameras in nearby properties, but none were covering the bit of land where Sonia’s body was found.

“It was in the middle of two rows of vines which were around 1.5 meters [just under 5ft] tall, so it was superficially hidden.



“This did not stop another vineyard worker spotting it immediately when he came into work first thing in the morning, when there was daylight.”

Other enquiry sources said Sonia had been spending a lot of time in Paris, which is some 550miles from her home city of Nice.

Pictures posted on her social media sites show her in cafés, restaurants and shops identified as being in the French capital.

Cécile Gensac, the Nimes public prosecutor who is leading the murder enquiry, has not yet disclosed the likely cause of Sonia’s death, but said her body was so badly brutalised that DNA was needed to identify it.

Ms Gensac confirmed “the theory that the murder was committed by a man known to the victim,” is the primary line of enquiry.



Nimes gendarmes managed to track down the prime suspect by analysing Sonia’s telephone call logs and then tracking vehicle movements on the night of the murder.

All of Sonia’s social media accounts have since been deleted, as police technology specialists search for online clues.

Sonia told friends she was represented by “an agency” in the Mediterranean city of Nice, and detectives are speaking to those who run it. It is thought to be one that specialises in online promotion.

A family friend said: “She was very independent – she did not rely on a boyfriend, or anyone else to look after her.

“She wasn’t known to have any particular romantic involvements, and she was never seen in late-night bars or clubs.



“She was anything but loud-mouthed or vulgar – quite the opposite.”

Police sources said Sonia did not have any criminal convictions, but had been a victim of assault and theft in the past. They could not provide any further details.

Mourad Battikh, the barrister representing the Bellina family, said he was preparing a legal complaint against people who had aimed “online insults” against Sonia’s memory.

“There is a hatred I can’t explain,” he said, adding: “All those who posted such remarks have been reported, and subsequently, complaints will be filed to ensure that these individuals, too, are brought before the courts.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Mourad suggested there “might be a link” between Sonia’s murder and the “hateful comments” she was already facing on social media while she was alive.



The two suspects in the case can be held until Friday, when magistrates will have to decide whether to charge them, release them, or request extra time to question them.

News.title: Huge search launched after lion ‘spotted’ in Spain as helicopters and drones take to sky to find killer beast
News.content:
A LION has allegedly been spotted prowling in the mountains of a Brit holiday hotspot – sparking a huge search operation.

The Civil Guard have launched helicopters and drones in a desperate two-day hunt for the carnivorous beast across Toledo, Spain.



A delivery driver claims he saw the killer feline stalking through Sierra de San Vicente, central Spain on Wednesday at around 10:40am.

He immediately called the 112 emergency line – and the civil guard swiftly launched a full scale search for the lion on the loose.



The caller was on the TO-1375 road near the historic Piélago convent when he says he spotted the terrifying animal.

Several local regions issued warnings to residents, urging them to stay off secondary roads while authorities tracked down the wild beast.

El Real de San Vicente Town Hall posted to Facebook warning residents of a report “of a possible lion sighting near the convent in the mountains.”

“There is no further information at this time; please exercise extreme caution”, they added to the post on Thursday afternoon.

Emergency services swiftly contacted the closest zoo, about 15km away, to see if a large feline had escaped their premises.

“No animals are missing from our facilities”, said a spokesperson for Zoo Safari Fauna Aventura de Hinojosa de San Vicente, threatening legal action if anyone accused them otherwise.



None of the zoos or natural wildlife reserves in the wider surrounding area – including Madrid – had reported a missing lion.

Since the search started two days ago officials have yet to uncover any footprints or new sightings of the beast.

Cops also investigated whether the delivery driver had confused a large dog with a lion.



Officials tracked down owners of larger, more dangerous pets – like Tibetan mastiffs and German shepherds – but have so far been unable to confirm what type of animal the man first spotted.

Given the lack of evidence, the hunt has now been suspended.

The government delegation in Castilla-La Mancha – the region of the erroneous sighting – reminded the public calling a false alarm can be a crime for wasting emergency resources.

Remarkably, it is not the first time a lion was allegedly sighted in the Toledo mountains.

In 2017 a supposed lion was prowling in the valley of the Cañamares River, prompting another large-scale search operation.



But months later, in 2018, the Civil Guard confirmed the sighting was actually a black dog.

News.title: Couple force to rip down secret £500k house 12 years after lying to council that it was going to be ‘horse semen lab’
News.content:
NEIGH WAY Couple force to rip down secret £500k house 12 years after lying to council that it was going to be ‘horse semen lab’

A COUPLE have been forced to tear down their secret £500k house after telling the council they were building a specialist “stallion semen” horse lab.

The home has been completely flattened, 12 years after the couple got planning permission for a horse semen collection lab but built a house instead.



A planning inspector ruled that the unauthorised house at Valentine Stables in Great Abington, Cambridgeshire, must be knocked down last May.

It has now been razed to the ground after three months of demolition work.





The couple had been granted permission to build a stable block and a specialist “stallion semen” collection laboratory in 2014.

It was supposed to have a small upstairs flat to be used by lab workers.

The building was approved for countryside business use, set to have a reception, office, kitchenette, “analysis and lecture” lab, processing laboratory and staff changing room on the ground floor.

On the first floor, planning was approved for a staff living space made up of two bedrooms with ensuites and a kitchen/living space.



But what was actually built was completely different.

From the outside, it looked like the building had followed the approved plans.

Inside, however, the building looked nothing like the approved plans for the lab and business, an investigation showed.



The planning inspector said the house had been used as a residential home from the start, with no evidence that the lab was ever built or used.

The council first ordered its demolition in July 2023. The couple appealed the decision, but in 2025 a planning inspector upheld the council’s ruling and ordered the house be torn down.

He highlighted the fact the couple had sold their old home and moved in to what was supposed to be a business site.

Inspector Chris Preston said there was no lab or business running at the site, nor any evidence to show there ever was.

He said there was also very little evidence that the stallion semen and collection business had “ever got off the ground to any notable degree.”



Preston said: “The lack of any clear record of the semen collection and analysis business, when added to the evidence that the laboratory and associated storage and analysis areas were never constructed raises serious doubts as to whether the 2014 permission was implemented.

“If the pandemic did cause issues with the business, the logical thing to do, if implementing the approved planning permission, would have been to construct the building as permitted, with accommodation at first floor level and space for the laboratories etc at ground floor level, even if that led to a delay in installation of those facilities.

“What actually appears to have happened is that the appellant constructed a dwelling from the off.”

He explained that photos “show a complete absence of any laboratory space or research facility”.

Preston added: “Throughout, the ground floor is decorated and equipped in a manner that belies a residential use. There is no obvious reception area that would indicate use by customers of a business.



“No laboratory has been installed, no research or stored equipment associated with the business is apparent, either on the photographs from 2022 or at the time of my visit.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Upstairs, where the staff accommodation was intended to be, there are two bedrooms, in the locations shown on the approved plans and a living area/ lounge, equipped with a sofa and television.

“However, no kitchen appears to have been constructed on the upper floor. In other words, the living space is clearly spread over the two floors, as would be the case in a typical house.”

News.title: Harry and Meghan's return to UK reignites questions over security
News.content:
In terms of why they were moving now, a source close to the couple said the "stars had aligned" at this time to make the move work for their family.

They are described by the source as an international couple who love to travel - and for the next while they are going to be based in the UK.

As well as surprising the world's media, it was also news to King Charles, who was told about the move on Sunday. He is said to be looking forward to seeing them more often.

The decision follows a visit in July by Prince Harry, Meghan and their children to see the King at his Highgrove home in Gloucestershire.

It was the first time the King had seen his grandchildren in person in more than four years, and the couple's first visit to the UK together since 2022.

It has also been two-and-a-half years since the King was diagnosed with cancer and in Prince Harry's BBC interview last year, he spoke of wanting to spend more time with his father.

Highgrove has the feel of a family home rather than a royal palace - and royal author Valentine Low says a key driver of their return has been the chance for Harry to rebuild links to his family and particularly to "repair his relationship with his father".

The couple will still keep their California home and Meghan's work in the media and her online food business, As Ever, can be carried out from a base in the UK as readily as in the US.

Next year, Prince Harry's Invictus Games are being held in Birmingham, which would have meant extensive travelling to meetings and events in the UK.

It will also mark the 30th anniversary of the death of his mother, Princess Diana, which will bring commemorations and events in the UK.

This summer saw Prince Harry and his family staying at the Spencer family home at Althorp and returning to the UK will be a chance to be closer to his mother's side of his family.

News.title: Five key takeaways from GCSE results day 2026
News.content:
You might be forgiven for glancing at this year's GCSE results and thinking not much has changed.

And sure, if you're just looking at the pass rate across England, Wales and Northern Ireland, that would be more or less correct.

But, when you dig into the detail, you'll find a more complicated picture, where some issues from last year have become even more stark.

You'll see the grades of students resitting their English and maths GCSEs in England are dragging down the overall results in those subjects - all part of a system the government itself says is "demoralising" and needs fixing.

You'll see that boys' and girls' grades are looking more similar - though that's more to do with girls slipping than boys improving.

And you'll see that, despite the government's pledges to "tackle entrenched inequality", the regional divide in England has actually grown, and remains stubbornly higher than it was before Covid.

Here are five key things you need to know.

News.title: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by university
News.content:
An academic who accused the late Cambridge professor Jason Arday of plagiarism has been suspended from his post at a Belgian university.

Nathan Cofnas, a self-defined "race realist", was among those to question Arday's work and achievements - prompting a weeks-long plagiarism row prior to his death on 14 August.

Cofnas said he was under investigation by Ghent University "for discriminating against Arday".

The university said a staff member had been notified of a "preliminary disciplinary investigation" and suspended as a precaution.

In a statement regarding Arday's death, its rector Petra De Sutter and vice-rector Herwig Reynaert said they took "recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously", and had taken "appropriate action".

They said the university stood for "respect for human dignity and opposes discrimination, hatred and racism".

"We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.

"It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others."

They said Arday's death should "prompt reflection" and that lessons should be learned "regarding the way we treat one another both within and outside the academic world, particularly when people become the subject of public controversy".

Cofnas works as a postdoctoral researcher at the university's department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website.

His role at a Cambridge college was terminated in 2024 after backlash to his view that, under a true meritocracy, black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

News.title: John Swinney defends £45,000 business-class flights to World Cup
News.content:
John Swinney has defended the use of more than Â£45,000 of public funds on business-class flights for him and two senior aides to the World Cup.

Scotland's first minister flew to Boston on 11 June for Scotland's opening match, before taking part in trade talks in Kentucky three days later.

While he and two senior officials travelled business class, Sports Minister Maree Todd and several other officials went to the US on significantly cheaper economy-class flights.

Swinney insisted the government had sought to "minimise" costs, while Justice Secretary Neil Gray defended the business class flights as a means of ensuring ministers "arrive fresh" when they travel overseas.

In total, the government spent Â£98,442 on trips for Swinney, Todd and their officials to the US, including flights, hotels and expenses.

Flights for Swinney and his private secretary John Webster cost Â£17,893 each.

Business-class tickets for the first minister's special adviser Colin McAllister cost Â£9,864.

News.title: Belgian car salesman becomes prince after royal parentage confirmed
News.content:
Belgium's Prince Laurent has legally recognised 26-year-old former car salesman ClÃ©ment Vandenkerckhove as his son and heir.

Vandenkerckhove, the result of a relationship between the royal and Belgian singer Wendy Van Wanten, was quietly brought into Prince Laurent's family at a town hall ceremony six months ago, although details have only just emerged.

While he formally becomes a prince, he will not receive a royal allowance.

The new prince has had several years to get used to the idea of having a royal father, and he said recently he was not yet sure he would begin using his father's name Saxe-Coburg.

"I might want to do that, but I am proud of the name Vandenkerckhove," he told Het Nieuwsblad.

"If I were to sacrifice that family name, it would be a betrayal of everything my mother has done for me."

He will not be part of Belgium's royal line of succession, unlike his half-sister Princess Louise and half-brothers Prince Aymeric and Prince Nicolas. Nor will he take part in public royal activities.

Vandenkerckhove is already well known to Belgians, having been the focus of a Flemish TV documentary last September, in which he described how he got to know his father.

His father had been in a relationship with Wendy Van Wanten, whose real name is Iris Vandenkerckhove, before he went on to marry Princess Claire in 2003.

During the VTM documentary, ClÃ©ment described meeting the prince unexpectedly in a shopping centre in 2013, without realising who he was. It was only when he was 16 that his mother revealed his father's identity.

Four years later he plucked up the courage to ring him up, and after several more calls they met in person and eventually Prince Laurent suggested they take a DNA test.

"We went to the hospital together and I remember him saying 'I'll go first so you're feeling at ease'," he told VTM. Then he received an email from the laboratory which told him of a 99.5% DNA match.

Prince Laurent's DNA test is reminiscent of his father, former King Albert II, who had a test after a lengthy paternity battle. Albert admitted in 2020 that he had fathered a daughter during an affair and eventually recognised her as his own.

Albert II abdicated as king of the Belgians in 2013 as the paternity issue became a royal scandal.

Delphine BoÃ«l, a well-known artist, eventually won her court battle and gained the right to the title of princess, and now calls herself Delphine de Saxe-Coburg.

Under changes to Belgian law in 2013, only a few members of the royal family are entitled to public allowances - King Philippe, his father King Albert II, Prince Laurent and Princess Astrid.

News.title: BBC DJ Trevor Nelson reveals brain tumour surgery 'went well'
News.content:
BBC DJ and presenter Trevor Nelson has revealed he stepped away from work after being diagnosed with a brain tumour.

Nelson was last on air in June and had announced he was "taking a little break from my work commitments" due to "health issues".

Speaking to his Instagram followers, external, the 62-year-old said that his "world was turned upside down" when a brain tumour was discovered.

He said that he had undergone a "very serious surgery" which "went incredibly well".

Speaking on Instagram on Thursday, Nelson explained: "There's been a lot of speculation as to what's wrong with me, I know that much. My phone's blown up 20 times over with people asking what's wrong with me.

"I felt that I should at least tell you what was wrong with me. I'm not going to go into it all now and I will deep dive into it at a later date so you can hear the full story."

He continued: "I'll tell you this, I was minding my own business and then it was discovered I had a brain tumour.

"I was shocked, my world was turned upside down, it was a shock to myself and close family and friends and you can imagine quite literally my head was all over the place."

News.title: Man charged over Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
A man has been charged in connection with the Manchester synagogue attack in which two men were killed.

Counter terrorism police said Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, 49, of St James Road, Higher Broughton, Salford, had been charged with failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity.

Hakim has been remanded into custody to appear before Westminster Magistrates' Court on Friday.

There have so far been eight arrests in connection with the attack, however this is the first charge that "relates directly" to the morning of 2 October, when two men died as the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation synagogue was attacked by Jihad Al-Shamie. He was shot by police and died at the scene.

Worshippers Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, were killed.

Assistant Chief Constable Rob Potts, from Counter Terrorism Policing North West (CTPNW) , said: "This is a significant development in our investigation, and my thoughts are with all those affected by the attack, particularly the bereaved loved ones and survivors.

"We have updated them and continue to offer them as much support as possible.

"Since the attack took place, we have been unwavering in our commitment to establishing the full picture behind the incident and identifying anybody who may have been involved in any way."

In July, Mohammad Bashir, 31, who planned an attack on a military base with the Manchester synagogue attacker was jailed for life with a minimum term of 17 years.

He drove his friend Jihad Al-Shamie on a 10-hour round trip to conduct hostile reconnaissance at the UK's Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Oxfordshire, on 14 August 2025.

Weeks after that journey, Al-Shamie, 35, was shot dead by police after carrying out the Heaton Park Synagogue attack.

News.title: 'Relentless' GCSE resit cycle 'simply not working', school and college leaders say
News.content:
The "relentless" cycle of pupils in England failing and then resitting their GCSEs in maths and English is "simply not working", a leading education union has said.

The Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL) said a "significant proportion" of students fall short of passing those subjects, and that most who retake those exams "face the miserable experience of falling short once again".

Thursday's results data showed nearly one in four maths and English GCSEs in England were taken by students aged 17 and older, mostly young people resitting exams they had previously failed.

The government said it wanted to stop the "endless treadmill of unnecessary resits".

It said it would introduce a new "stepping stone" qualification from 2028 at Level 1 - one level below GCSEs - for students who do not achieve a pass in GCSE maths or English.

Currently, many courses and jobs remain dependent on students securing GCSE passes in those subjects.

But those that miss the grade can find themselves in a continuing loop of resits as they try and try again to pass.

Pepe Di'Iasio, general secretary of ASCL, said the fail-resit cycle was like "force feeding" students a "relentless diet of GCSE English and maths".

"This limits their education and career options and is very likely to be a factor in the large number of young people who end up not in employment, education or training," he said.

Pass rates for students aged 17 and older in English and maths are much lower than 16-year-old students taking the exams for the first time, bringing down overall GCSE grades for all ages across England, Wales and Northern Ireland as a result.

News.title: People smuggler exposed by BBC investigation arrested and charged
News.content:
A convicted people smuggler who was found by the BBC to be living in Leicestershire has been arrested and charged with immigration offences.

Twana Jamal Khdir, an Iraqi national who was once described as "the godfather" of the French migrant camps, previously served a sentence for people smuggling in France.

Last month, the BBC revealed he was now living in the UK.

The BBC has been told he was arrested on Tuesday near Uppingham in a joint operation led by the Midlands Criminal Financial Investigations team, with the support of Leicestershire Police.

He was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service and appeared at Leicester Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

He pleaded guilty to entering the UK without valid entry clearance, but not guilty to seeking to obtain leave to enter or remain by deceptive means.

He has been remanded in custody and will next appear at Leicester Crown Court on 5 October.

Khdir was given a five-year jail sentence in France in 2016, where authorities described him as one of the most successful people smugglers ever caught.

Prosecutors said the Iraqi Kurd, aged 36 at the time, had earned up to Â£100,000 a week for moving illegal immigrants across the Channel.

News.title: Thunderstorm warnings expire but rain continues to bring risk of floods for UK
News.content:
Heavy showers and thunderstorms will continue to affect large swathes of the UK on Thursday afternoon, bringing the threat of flooding and travel disruption.

A Met Office yellow thunderstorm covering parts of northern England and north Wales expired at 13:00 BST, with focus of heavy downpours shifting southwards across England and Wales.

Drivers are still being warned that wet weather could lead to slippery conditions and flooded roads.

The Environment Agency has issued one flood warning, external for Walverdon Water in Nelson, Lancashire.

Temperatures are also dropping with some places expected to remain below the August average over the next few days.

News.title: Vapes could lead to health harms in children, doctors warn
News.content:
Vaping could lead to health harms in children and young people and should be made "less attractive" to them, doctors have said.

The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) has reviewed about 81 studies into vaping and said it is linked to higher rates of breathing problems and evidence of harm in babies whose mothers used vapes while pregnant.

The review said vaping should not be seen as a "harmless part of growing up".

The RCPCH is calling on the UK government to go further in its proposals to place new restrictions around the sale of vapes and suggests limiting the number of flavours that are available.

The review into vapes has been published in the journal Archives of Disease in Childhood. Experts from the college looked at the studies involving health or social outcomes of vaping on children and young people.

It said vaping had an association with problems including wheezing and coughing, poor oral and dental health, poor sleep, mental health problems and eye symptoms.

Co-author of the systematic review, Prof Will Carroll, said the evidence showed "clear links" with respiratory symptoms, nicotine dependence and subsequent cigarette smoking.

"We must act to make vaping less attractive and accessible to children," he said.

Vice-president for policy of the RCPCH, Dr Mike McKean, added: "Vaping is still a relatively new product, and there is much we do not yet know about its long-term impact on children and young people but a clear and concerning picture is emerging."

"We need to keep pace with a rapidly evolving market and continue to take action to protect children from nicotine products."

In July, the government launched a 12-week consultation on the appearance, packaging and display of vapes with the aim of reducing the appeal of the products to children.

As part of the new proposals, packs would need to be plain with strict limits on branding and only simple flavour descriptions like "apple" or "cola" used.

Other restrictions would move vapes out of sight in shops, similar to how cigarettes and tobacco are currently sold.

The 100-day consultation follows the recent passing of the Tobacco and Vapes Act,, external which sets out proposals to create the UK's first smoke-free generation.

Children aged 17 or younger now face a lifelong ban on buying cigarettes, since it will be illegal for shops to sell tobacco to anyone born after 1 January 2009.

Dr McKean said the new act was "an important step towards protecting children from nicotine addiction, but it must not be seen as a one-and-done solution".

Prof Carroll said the government needed "to go further and limit the types of flavours available to them as opposed to just their descriptions".

News.title: School 'deeply saddened' by death of family in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
A school attended by a 14-year-old girl who died alongside her father and mother after getting into difficulty in water off the coast of Shoreham-by-Sea has paid tribute to her.

Sara El-Khawas and her parents, husband and wife Hassan El-Khawas, 55, and Zeina Alayn, 37, are believed to have gone into the water near Shoreham Fort in West Sussex on Tuesday, according to Sussex Police.

In a statement on its website, the Ellen Wilkinson School for Girls in Ealing, west London, described Sara as a "sweet girl, well-liked by staff and students".

A fourth member of the family, a younger girl, remains in hospital in a critical condition, police confirmed on Thursday.

News.title: Burnham announces plans to clean up worst three illegal waste dumps
News.content:
Three of the country's worst illegal dumps are due to be cleaned up using taxpayers' money, the government has announced.

Sites in Kent, Surrey and West Yorkshire will be assessed for clearance, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham saying the "toxic dumps have blighted communities for too long".

Fines for waste offences will also rise from Â£300 to Â£5,000 to deter, catch, and punish those who dump illegally, and the Environment Agency will have more powers to seize assets bought with the proceeds of crime by those involved.

But opposition parties said illegal dumps were a small part of a much bigger issue with smaller scale fly-tipping and landfill all posing big problems for communities.

Burnham is looking to build on work started by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer to tackle waste crime, with an action plan published in March detailing a series of measures - including using drones to map illegal waste sites.

Sir Keir's administration had announced that sites in Wigan, Sheffield and Lancashire would have government clean-ups - alongside Kidlington in Oxfordshire where removal of 20,000 tonnes of waste started in April.

The government said the new sites identified for clearance contain around 22,000 tonnes of illegally dumped waste.

They are: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road in Bradford, West Yorkshire.

West Yorkshire and Greater Manchester will be the first areas with new region-led approaches to waste crime.

The government said this will give mayors and council leaders the lead in co-ordinating councils, police, regulators, and other enforcement agencies.

Speaking on a visit to the waste dump in West Yorkshire, Burnham said: "We've begun a much more networked approach to this, where we're bringing the National Crime Agency in to work with the Environment Agency, increasing the penalties and bearing down now on the organised crime that lies behind some of what you see behind me."

The prime minister said the aim was to build intelligence about criminals linked to waste dumps at an earlier stage, to avoid the public being charged for clean-ups.

"We should be getting in much earlier, apprehending them, using all of the intelligence that comes through that investigation to make sure the polluter pays," he added.

A new "waste crime crackdown group", chaired by Environment Secretary Angela Eagle, will bring regulators and law enforcement together in a bid to dismantle criminal operations.

Eagle said: "We are cleaning up sites, but we are also stopping the cycle, driving faster prevention and disruption, better intelligence, and stronger coordination across the system."

News.title: Reform UK proposes tax rebates for firms to boost apprenticeships
News.content:
Young apprentices should have part of their wages paid by taxpayers, according to Reform UK plans, external aimed at delivering a "skills revolution".

The party's education spokeswoman Suella Braverman said a Reform government would introduce an "apprenticeship wage credit" offering small and medium-sized businesses a 30% rebate on the wages of apprentices they take on aged 16 to 18.

She also advised students receiving their GCSE exam results on Thursday "not to get ripped off by the great university scam" and to learn a trade instead.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he wants teenagers to have technical routes into careers that could rival the path of a traditional university degree.

The government has been introducing changes and examining ways to encourage more young people into work, including giving some parents on benefits up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships.

Former minister Alan Milburn has been tasked with investigating why so many young people are not in employment, education or training - known by the acronym Neets.

Reform said its announcement was the first in a series of proposals aimed at reaching 600,000 apprenticeship starts per year by the end of the next Parliament, likely to be 2034.

The party says it would pay for its plans by banning all foreign students from accessing taxpayer-funded loans and stopping what the party calls "Mickey Mouse degrees".

Reform said its policy, which also includes a Â£2,000 retention bonus for apprentices, could cost between Â£1.48bn and almost Â£2bn over five years.

Braverman said there are "excessive number of graduates with qualifications that don't match the skills needed for our country," arguing that learning a trade would be a better use of their time.

Apprentices are generally paid a lower wage but get on-the-job training and practical work experience.

Speaking at a press conference, Braverman said: "We're firing the starting gun on unleashing a technical and vocational renaissance of homegrown skills.

"Reform will not do this because it fills us with some jingoistic pride but because we will do what it takes to save Britain from the perpetual doom loop of decline, debt and despair that we're currently in."

The MP said the apprenticeship wage credit would result in businesses saving an average of Â£4,000-a-year per apprentice.

The Â£2,000 tax-free retention bonus would be paid to workers who "show loyalty" by staying with the business that trained them for at least two years after they complete their apprenticeship, said Braverman.

Asked if the policy would mean some universities would have to close, Braverman said she did not envisage that but instead suggested universities need to "repurpose" themselves into construction colleges and manufacturing colleges.

When pressed to give examples of "Mickey Mouse degrees", Braverman pointed to "gender studies" and "golf course studies".

She said: "There's not a necessity, there's not a value in many of these degrees."

The British and International Golf Greenkeepers Association (BIGGA) has previously criticised Braverman for similar remarks, which they branded "negligent and potentially damaging".

BIGGA chief executive Jim Croxton said: "Golf course management is a growing industry with currently more vacancies than qualified applicants.

"Anyone successfully studying for a degree in this field is effectively guaranteed employment in a vibrant industry."

A Labour Party spokesperson said all young people "deserve a clear route to a good career" whether through "a properly funded apprenticeship, high-quality technical education or university".

The spokesperson added: "That's exactly what this Labour government is already delivering, with 500,000 new jobs, apprenticeships and training opportunities to help young people earn or learn, including a guaranteed job for 18â24-year-olds who have been out of work for 18 months."

On Wednesday, Conservative shadow education secretary Laura Trott said there is demand for apprenticeships but claimed the Labour government "aren't doing enough to boost supply".

She said: "Our New Deal for Young People would axe the dead end degrees that don't lead to jobs and instead invest in apprenticeships giving school leavers more choice."

Liberal Democrat universities spokesperson Ian Sollom said it was important to protect local colleges and universities as well as boosting apprenticeships, including apprenticeships in degree courses.

"Reform's proposals amount to dangerous economic vandalism which would rip a multi-billion-pound hole in our world-leading university sector," he added.

Green Party MP Hannah Spencer, who was a plumber before becoming an MP, said: "People are tired of Reform pitting us against each other - Those of us that did apprenticeships can still see the value in degrees and everyone should be able to choose their own path of education."

She added the Greens had announced a windfall tax on big banks, which she said would support small businesses employing more young people.

News.title: Rare Suffragette Christmas card from 1910 found at roadshow
News.content:
A rare Suffragette Christmas card from around 1910 has been discovered at a vintage roadshow.

The card, found in Mold, Flintshire, and which comes from the height of the campaign to win women the vote, was produced to raise funds and awareness for the movement.

Today, surviving examples are "exceptionally scarce", according to antique shop WeBuyVintage, which has valued the item at Â£2,500.

"These weren't simply Christmas cards, they were pieces of political campaigning that helped fund one of the most significant social movements in British history," said Matt Case, an antiques specialist.

Case said that finding an original Suffragette Christmas card was "incredibly exciting".

Because they were intended to be seasonal and disposable, "very few have survived, especially in such good condition", he added.

Sold by organisations such as the Women's Social and Political Union (WSPU), they helped finance the campaign while keeping the movement visible during the Christmas season.

Museums, including the London Museum, external, now hold examples in their permanent collections as important artefacts documenting the fight for women's voting rights.

In Wales, Lady Rhondda, born Margaret Haig-Thomas, led a 40-year campaign for women to be allowed to sit in the House of Lords - although she died just before the law she fought for was changed, too late to take her own seat.

President Donald Trump’s construction challenges are piling up at home – and abroad – with the planned design of a 12,000 square-foot ballroom at his golf course in Ireland hitting a sluggish holdup from a local man.

The planned construction of the “nicest ballroom in the country,” according to the president’s son Eric Trump, was supposed to be the latest addition to the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, a small village of roughly 300 people in County Clare.

But Liam Madden, a man living in Longford with a penchant for appealing development projects around Ireland, is holding up construction by claiming the plans failed to comply with regulations, The Washington Post reported.

Madden asserts that helicopter landing areas at the resort were not considered in an environmental impact assessment – which could hurt the area’s protected snail species.

“I’ve caught them with their pants down,” Madden, 76, told the Washington Post in a July interview.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump hopes to build a 320-seat ballroom at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, Ireland ( PA Archive )

The challenge to Trump’s ballroom in Doonbeg comes at an ironic moment when the president is facing similar pushback to his 90,000 square-foot ballroom attached to the White House.

Unlike in the U.S., where federal judges have expressed concern about the construction but largely allowed it to continue, the Doonbeg ballroom is likely facing a drawn-out challenge.

The Independent has asked the Trump Organization for comment.

Last year, Eric Trump, the co-executive vice president of the Trump Organization, told the Sunday Independent that the ballroom would be “spectacular” and the nicest in all of Ireland.

“The design is the best you’ve ever seen. It’s really incredible, and I’m working on that very, very closely,” he said.

Most of Doonbeg’s residents appeared welcoming of the new ballroom, hoping it would bring tourism and economic prosperity to the area, locals told the Washington Post.

open image in gallery In Washington, DC, Trump hopes to build a 90,000 square-foot ballroom attached to the White House – so far, federal judges have largely allowed construction to continue despite concerns that he needs approval from Congress first ( AFP/Getty )

But Madden claims the planning documents failed to include two proposed helicopter landing pads, which were promoted in a marketing video, or measure their environmental impact.

Particularly, he argues, it could harm the population of the local protected snail.

The Vertigo angustior is a narrow-mouthed whorl snail that happens to reside in the marshy grasslands surrounding the golf course. When Trump bought the golf club property in 2014, he allegedly promised an environmentalist that he would “defend the snail.”

Tony Lowes, director of the Friends of the Irish Environment, a network of independent environmentalists, told Newsweek earlier this year that Trump has not held up his promise and the snail’s population is in “terminal decline.”

Madden’s appeal to the An Coimisiún Pleanála, the Irish planning appellate board, requests that they “refuse this nonsense,” referring to the proposed ballroom.

open image in gallery Locals of Doonbeg in Co. Clare, Ireland, reportedly welcomed the construction of a ballroom attached to Trump International Golf Links & Hotel (pictured center) ( PA Wire )

The Trump Organization has previously faced off against the snail – and Madden. In 2016, the Irish planning board sided with environmentalists and Madden when the Trumps tried to build a 1.7-mile rock barrier along the beach to protect the golf course from storm damage

But locals do not appear supportive of Madden’s latest appeal, with several telling the Washington Post they found it “totally unfair” and “disgraceful.”

But Madden told the newspaper he’s confident he will win.

“Joe Biden beat Donald Trump once,” Madden said. “I’ve beaten him twice.”

First Lady Melania Trump made her first public appearance in more than a month as she delivered remarks from the White House to tout her foster care initiative.

“I heard you missed me,” she said as she addressed a crowd at the Rose Garden on Thursday. “Here I am.”

The first lady has remained largely out of the spotlight with her husband’s return to the White House. She has made even fewer public appearances in the president’s second term than his first; her last public appearance was at the 2026 World Cup final on July 19.

Melania Trump did not join the president to attend the dignified transfer of the remains of four dead U.S. service members, nor did she sit beside the president at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner two days later on July 24.

She also did not attend Senator Lindsey Graham’s funeral on July 28.

( Getty )

An analysis from The Daily Beast determined Melania Trump, until her appearance at the White House on Thursday, had appeared in public only 38 days this year.

Trump aide Natalie Harp, meanwhile, has seldom strayed far from the president’s side.

The continued presence of the 35-year-old executive assistant within the president’s inner circle has come under intense scrutiny following reports that she was among a small group of top aides who secretly joined Trump aboard a military aircraft departing a NATO summit in Turkey this summer.

The former One America News Network personality reportedly declined to obtain security clearance for more than a year after she started working at the White house and repeatedly received extensions to complete the paperwork that would require her to disclose her financial history, prior residences and foreign contacts.

Recent remarks from Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff — who said Trump “doesn’t want to do the job” of president but would rather build a highly contentious White House ballroom and “travel with Natalie” — sparked a fierce defense of Harp’s presence from the president’s allies while amplifying questions about her role at the White House.

The first lady — in partnership with IndyCar and the Fox Corporation as the president launches a Grand Prix race in Washington, D.C. — announced the launch of a new scholarship program for young adults transitioning out of foster care.

Her “Fostering the Future” initiative is being supported by a $2 million donation from the companies to fund scholarships at Indiana University and Purdue University, according to the White House. The partnership expands the program’s network to 26 academic institutions.

“America's greatest competitive advantage remains in its own people,” she said in prepared remarks. “Tomorrow’s leaders are sitting in classrooms today, including those growing up in foster care. Their capability is no less remarkable.”

This is a developing story

News.title: Suspect who terrified joggers wearing creepy Chucky mask ID’d by cops as manhunt spreads nationwide
News.content:

The man accused of terrorizing multiple people in Philadelphia while wearing a Chucky mask and asking a jogger if she was “ready to die” has been identified by police.

Zymire Hughes, 22, is wanted on an active arrest warrant after he allegedly confronted at least six people near City Hall in Center City on August 12, Philadelphia police announced Thursday.

Hughes may have fled Pennsylvania and has ties to California and Nevada.

The U.S. Marshals Service is assisting in the search and working to return Hughes to Philadelphia. The suspect could face charges including harassment, terroristic threats, simple assault, reckless endangerment and intimidation, Philadelphia Police Capt. Jason Smith said Monday.

The creepy encounters began last Wednesday around 5:18 a.m. when a man dressed in dark clothing and wearing a Halloween-style Chucky doll mask was captured on surveillance footage approaching people on the street. Police said the incidents continued for about 20 minutes, with the masked man apparently attempting to frighten or antagonize people.

open image in gallery Zymire Hughes, 22, has been identified as the suspect who chased a Philadelphia jogger last week and allegedly terrorized at least six others ( Suspect who terrified joggers wearing creepy 'Chucky' mask ID'd by cops as manhunt spreads nationwide )

One encounter involved a 40-year-old female jogger near 15th Street and John F. Kennedy Boulevard. Hughes allegedly approached her while holding his cellphone toward her and repeatedly asked, “Are you ready to die?” He then chased her as she screamed for help.

“The female is screaming for help this entire time,” Smith said Monday, according to 6abc Action News. The man eventually stopped, headed north on 15th Street and entered Suburban Station via the escalators.

Smith said the jogger was the only person to have formally reported an encounter as of Monday, even though investigators believe the suspect had confronted at least six people.

One witness said the encounter seemed like “some twisted game” to the masked suspect.

“He starts asking, ‘Do you guys want to race me? I bet I am faster than you. Want to race me?’ He asked a few times, but none of us acknowledged him. Very weird,” Luanda Marinho told CBS News.

”We're scared, so now we're thinking about changing our routes or changing our schedules, which shouldn't be an issue,” she added. “It was just weird, like some twisted game."

open image in gallery Hughes, believed to be pictured here wearing the Chucky mask, could face charges including terroristic threats, harassment, simple assault, reckless endangerment and intimidation ( Philadelphia Police Department )

Another woman, identified only as Jameka, told 6abc that she encountered the suspect shortly before the jogger was chased. She spotted him approaching the runner near the La Colombe coffee shop and noticed the woman was wearing headphones. Jameka waved to get her attention and warned her that someone was behind her.

”I started to wave at her from across the intersection and say, 'Hey, there's someone behind you, look behind you,’” Jameka said. “And she heard me, and then she started to run away.”

Anyone with information on this case or Hughes is asked to contact the department at 215-686-TIPS (8477).

Amid a severe heatwave in Italy, exaggerated and inaccurate posts on social media have distorted the climate's effect on Parmigiano Reggiano cheese production and the financial institutions that hold the wheels as loan collateral.

Parmigiano Reggiano is crafted under precise standards within designated territories of the Emilia Romagna region in northern Italy. The milk comes strictly from dairy cows nourished on local feed, with each wheel undergoing an aging period lasting from 12 to 40 months.

To assist farmers with working capital during aging, select banks take the cheese wheels as collateral for loans. The largest facility handling this is Credito Emiliano S.p.A’s Magazini Generali delle Tagliate (MGT), which has operated since 1953.

Social media posts claimed that Italy's extreme temperatures were endangering both the traditional cheese and its primary storage bank.

A review of the facts reveals the true status of production and storage.

open image in gallery Social media posts claimed that Italy's extreme temperatures were endangering both the traditional cheese and its primary storage bank ( AFP via Getty Images )

Claim: High temperatures have triggered a "Great Parmesan Crisis" that threatens Parmigiano Reggiano cheese and the Italian "cheese banks" storing hundreds of thousands of wheels as collateral.

The Facts: The cheese wheels are safely stored inside cooled facilities, undisturbed by the heat outside. MGT, which houses 500,000 wheels worth 300 million euros ($350 million) across two sites, confirmed its facilities are functioning as normal.

Giancarlo Ravanetti, general manager of MGT, noted that summer temperatures repeatedly approaching 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) increased the electricity required to keep facilities cool by 30%.

However, he confirmed that MGT's operations and the stored cheese remain completely safe despite the heat.

"The warehouses have not been affected and have continued operating normally, ensuring the cheese wheels are stored and aged under optimal conditions," he said, adding that he expects no long-term problems should severe heat continue in future years.

MGT has spent several years upgrading its infrastructure for better energy efficiency. The company replaced two outdated cooling units with a high-efficiency system, enhanced building insulation, and set up rooftop solar panels across both sites to reach a 1.5 MW capacity.

The Parmigiano Reggiano consortium, the regulatory body overseeing the cheese, recognized heatwaves as a "long-standing challenge" that can suppress milk production, with "yields potentially falling by around 10%."

Even so, the group clarified in a statement that production "is not currently at risk."

The organization stressed that cows mostly consume preserved, dried feed to maintain nutrition during droughts. Furthermore, farms supplying 70% of the milk rely on fans, regulated water misting, and climate sensors to reduce heat stress, while the rest of the milk is gathered from cooler hill and mountain areas.

Just one sugar-laden soda a day leads to a higher risk of developing deadly stomach cancer, according to a groundbreaking new study.

Drinking at least one serving of beverages with high fructose corn syrup - including sodas, energy drinks and fruit juices - more than doubled the risk for the cancer compared to people who had less than one serving a month, according to Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute researchers, who studied data from 112,000 healthy U.S. adults.

There are 31,000 new cases of stomach cancer and 10,000 deaths expected from the illness this year, according to the American Cancer Society, but research into risk from sugary beverages has been limited.

“Gastric cancer is the fifth-leading cause of cancer death worldwide, but we’ve known very little about how diet might contribute to this cancer,” Dr. Andrew Chan, a gastroenterologist and epidemiologist at the institute, explained.

Some two-thirds of American adults report drinking these beverages daily.

open image in gallery Soft drinks sit in a cooler in San Francisco, California, in March 2013. New research shows an association between drinks with high fructose corn syrup and stomach cancer ( (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) )

While the researchers are still looking into why these beverages might increase the risk for stomach cancer, they hypothesize that it’s the high fructose corn syrup that’s the culprit. High fructose corn syrup is made from corn starch and also used in many processed and packaged foods, including baked goods, condiments and cereals.

Consuming high fructose corn syrup increases fat production and levels of harmful inflammation, both of which raise the risk of cancer, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

The inexpensive sweetener has previously been shown to indirectly fuel the growth of cancer tumors in mice.

The researchers think that it’s likely to blame in sodas because they ruled out the number one cause of stomach cancer cases, infections from the bacteria Helicobacter pylori . These infections in the lining of the stomach make up the majority of cases worldwide.

But by looking at a subset of nearly 1,000 participants of the study, the researchers found that some people had this bacteria - but they could find no association between drinking the beverages and becoming infected.

Artificial sweeteners, often used in diet sodas, did not show the same risk as fructose.

However, the study is unable to prove cause and effect yet, Chan told Fox News Digital Wednesday. "What we did see was an association. We certainly need to do more research to understand whether this association between sugary-sweetened beverages and stomach cancer is truly causal,” he said.

open image in gallery The bacteria Helicobacter Pylori is seen in this graphic image looking inside a person's stomach. The bacteria is known as the number one cause of stomach cancer ( National Cancer Institute/iStock )

It’s not just drinks that could be raising peoples’ risk for stomach cancer, too. Poor nutrition and lifestyle habits have long been linked to heightened risk.

Eating food that’s been pickled in a salty brine, eating meat that’s been processed, grilled or charbroiled and not eating enough fruits increases the risk of developing the cancer, the American Cancer Society says.

Fortunately, stomach cancer is one of the rarer cancers in the U.S. - making up just 1.5 percent of new yearly cases - and avoiding these foods and drinks can help lower risk.

News.title: More than 2,300 Mexicans sent to Guatemala and Honduras as Trump ramps up third-country deportations
News.content:
