World.title: Tesco Teams Up With Wolt. Can Express Delivery Save Its Czech Business?
World.content:
Tesco will launch a new express delivery service in Prague in September, working with Wolt to deliver orders within 40 minutes.

The service, called Tesco Hned, will initially be available from selected Tesco stores in the Czech capital.

The launch comes as speculation continues over a possible sale of Tesco’s Central European operations and the British retailer’s future in the Czech Republic.



Tesco Hned is designed for customers who need groceries and other everyday products quickly rather than as part of a larger planned shop. Orders will include food, drinks, cosmetics, household products, pet supplies and other goods.

The company says its standard online shopping service will continue to focus on larger orders, while the new option is aimed at customers who need a few items immediately.

Tesco has already tested the service at six Prague stores. It plans to extend Tesco Hned to another 22 locations in the coming weeks.

Delivery will be provided through Wolt, giving customers access to Tesco products through the courier company’s platform.

Tesco faces questions over its future

The new service comes at a difficult time for Tesco in Central Europe.

According to the Financial Times, Tesco’s British owners are considering selling their operations in the region, including the Czech Republic. The Schwarz Group, which owns Lidl and Kaufland, and Polish retailer Biedronka have reportedly been mentioned among potential buyers.

Tesco has not announced plans to leave the Czech market, and the launch of Tesco Hned suggests the company continues to invest in its services.

World.title: New Budget Airline to Launch Direct Flights from Prague to Santiago de Compostela
World.content:
A new budget airline is set to launch direct flights between Prague and Santiago de Compostela in Spain, giving travellers from the Czech capital a new low-cost option for visiting Galicia and the famous Camino de Santiago.

Fly2Galicia plans to begin operating flights from Santiago–Rosalía de Castro Airport to eight European destinations from December 1, 2026.



Prague is among the international destinations, alongside Brussels, Munich, Venice and Milan.

Tickets are already on sale, with fares from Prague to Santiago de Compostela starting at €51.

The new route could be particularly attractive in 2027, when Santiago de Compostela will celebrate a Holy Year. The occasion is expected to bring increased numbers of pilgrims completing the Camino de Santiago, one of Europe’s best-known pilgrimage routes.

There is, however, one detail to note: Fly2Galicia will not operate the initial flights itself. The airline says the routes will be operated by another European carrier, which has not yet been named.

The new service comes as airlines continue to expand connections between Central Europe and Spain. Wizz Air has also announced new flights to Santiago from Rome and Warsaw starting this December.

What to see in Santiago de Compostela

For travellers arriving from Prague, Santiago’s historic centre is the main attraction. Its UNESCO-listed Old Town combines Romanesque, Gothic, Baroque and Neoclassical architecture, with the Cathedral of Santiago at the heart of the city.

The Mercado de Abastos is another popular stop, offering fresh seafood and local produce. Galicia is also known for Albariño, a white wine that pairs particularly well with the region’s seafood.

Santiago can also serve as a base for exploring Galicia, with trips to A Coruña, Vigo and the Rías Baixas wine region, as well as the area’s beaches and islands.

World.title: Russell Crowe to Perform in Prague for the First Time in May 2027
World.content:
Oscar-winning actor and musician Russell Crowe will bring his band, The Gentlemen Barbers, to Forum Karlín on May 23, 2027, for their first-ever Prague concert.

Russell Crowe is best known for his roles in Gladiator, A Beautiful Mind and A Good Year, but long before Hollywood, music was a major part of his life.

On May 23, 2027, the Oscar and Golden Globe winner will bring that side of his career to Prague for the first time, performing with his band The Gentlemen Barbers at Forum Karlín.



You can get your ticket here.

The concert will also mark the opening night of the band’s European tour.

The Gentlemen Barbers have been developing their sound over the past four years, although many of the musicians have worked with Crowe for decades. The lineup includes drummer Dave Kelly and trumpeter Stewart Kirwan, both former members of Thirty Odd Foot of Grunts, as well as musicians who have collaborated with Crowe on later projects.

The band also features pianist Stu Hunter, guitarist Chris Kamzelas and bassist James Hazelwood. Irish singer Lorraine O’Reilly, known for her powerful, raspy vocals, has performed with Crowe since they first met while recording a duet for the Bible Code Sundays album Walk Like Kings.

The result is a band that moves between R&B, gospel, country, dark waltzes and singalong anthems, with storytelling at the centre of its music.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JV Classics (@jvclassics)

“There is an attitude about this band. It’s got a groove. We do a lot of story songs, but we also know we are here to blow out cobwebs and give the audience a good night,” Crowe says.

For Crowe, music has remained a constant alongside his film career. He began performing in bands, touring and releasing records before moving into musical theatre and eventually film. He has continued to perform throughout his decades in Hollywood, despite his demanding acting career.

“I love playing in pubs. It’s what I did growing up. Even though my day job has a huge claim on my time, I’ve never not played music,” he says.

Russell Crowe’s Indoor Garden Party & The Gentlemen Barbers takes place on May 23, 2027, at 8 p.m. at Forum Karlín in Prague.

World.title: Students in Czech Republic Face Higher Rents as Housing Costs Rise
World.content:
Students looking for private accommodation in Czech university cities this year are facing higher rents, with prices for some types of housing up by as much as 14 percent compared with 2025.

The increase comes as demand for student accommodation reaches its annual peak ahead of the winter semester.

Data from several Czech property platforms show that the busiest period started earlier this year, meaning students who have not yet found accommodation may face a more limited and expensive selection in September.

Those unable to secure a place in a student dormitory generally have three alternatives: renting a small apartment alone, taking a private room in a shared apartment, or renting a bed in shared accommodation.



The most expensive option is usually a small one-bedroom apartment with a kitchenette, typically around 30 square meters. According to the REMAX network, monthly rents for these apartments range from more than CZK 7,000 in Ústí nad Labem to around CZK 14,000 in Prague.

Prices have not increased evenly across the country. Brno recorded the sharpest rise, with rents for small apartments increasing by 12 percent year on year.

Prague saw a 4 percent increase, while rents in Hradec Králové and Pardubice rose by almost 9 percent. Olomouc was one of the few exceptions, with prices falling by slightly more than 2 percent.

Rent is not the only expense students need to consider. Utilities, water and maintenance charges can add another CZK 1,000 to CZK 2,000 a month, according to property platforms.

Private rooms offer a cheaper alternative

Many students instead rent individual rooms in shared apartments, with properties ranging from smaller 2+kk and 2+1 layouts to larger 4+kk and 4+1 apartments. Czech property portal Sreality.cz puts the average cost of a private room in university cities at between approximately CZK 5,700 in Opava and CZK 11,500 in Prague.

In Prague, private rooms listed on Sreality.cz were around 10 percent more expensive than during the same period last year. Prices in Brno, meanwhile, remained roughly unchanged.

Shared housing remains the cheapest option

For students on a tighter budget, sharing an apartment and renting a bed rather than an entire room remains the least expensive choice. The more people share a property, the lower the individual housing costs tend to be.

Even this option, however, has become more expensive. According to UlovDomov.cz, the cost of renting a bed has increased by several hundred Czech crowns compared with last year.

Prague remains considerably more expensive. A bed in a two-bedroom apartment costs almost CZK 5,500, about CZK 1,200 more than a bed in a three-bedroom apartment.

World.title: 58 Years Since Warsaw Pact Troops Invaded Czechoslovakia
World.content:
On August 21, 1968, Soviet troops and their Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia to bring an end to that country’s brief period of political liberalization, called the Prague Spring.

People still recall waking up on that fateful morning to find that Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks had rolled into the country, crushing all hope of implementing the democratic reforms of the Prague Spring. Shocked citizens took to the streets in protest of the invasion.

About 500,000 troops were involved in the invasion and occupation, during which 137 Czechoslovaks died and some 500 were wounded.

One of the key battles was for the control of Czech Radio, similar to the one that took place at the end of the Second World War.

The invasion ended the political and economic reforms led by Alexander Dubcek and reasserted dominant Soviet and Communist authority in Czechoslovakia.

It also helped establish the Brezhnev Doctrine, which Moscow said allowed the U.S.S.R. to intervene in any country where a communist government was under threat.

Within the following year, resistance faded, Dubček was removed from office, his reforms were undone, and a more Soviet-controlled government was installed.

World.title: Prague’s Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
World.content:
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.

Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.

According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.



The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.

From Barcelona to Prague

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.

Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.

After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.

The First Edition

Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.

Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.

Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.

Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.

Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Rubio praises US-Hungary ties as Orbán, Karácsony deliver starkly different messages on 20 August holiday
World.content:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio praised the strong partnership between the United States and Hungary in a message marking Hungary’s national holiday, published on the State Department’s website on Thursday.

Rubio noted that 20 August was a reminder “of the historic ties between our peoples”. “The friendship between the United States and Hungary rests on the foundation of a mutual respect for sovereignty, proud heritage, and the hard-won liberties that define our two republics,” he added.

“Today, the United States reaffirms its strong and forward-looking partnership with Hungary, one sustained by deep economic ties, shared security interests, and a commitment to the values that have long united the West,” Rubio wrote.

Karácsony wishes Hungary happy ‘rebirthday’ on national holiday

Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony marked the 20 August national holiday on Thursday by wishing Hungary a “happy rebirthday” and highlighted the need to strengthen the resilience of Hungary and Budapest.

“Happy birthday, Hungary! But perhaps, here and now, it would be more accurate to say: happy rebirthday, Hungary!’ Karácsony said in a video on his YouTube channel, noting that an overwhelming majority had voted for a “European Hungary” in the April election.

Speaking about the challenges facing the country, Karácsony noted that the water level of the Danube had never been so low, the summer had never been so hot or so dry, and the country’s water and electricity supplies had never been so close to collapse as during this summer.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

The heat, the drought and their serious consequences will not be exceptions, but the new norm in Hungary, and in Budapest in particular, he said. The number of hot days is steadily rising, and “we are having to contend with prolonged droughts or sudden floods”, which are affecting agriculture, housing, transport, health and the social situation, he said.

The sight of the Danube, Lake Velence, Lake Balaton, the rivers and streams, the arable fields and the parks had perhaps made it clear to everyone that this was not merely a scientific prediction, nor was it scaremongering, he said. Constant adaptation, as well as strengthening the resilience of the country and of Budapest – which is particularly vulnerable to climate change – is the responsibility of the government, the capital, all Hungarian local authorities and every Hungarian citizen, he added.

Orbán: ‘We were, we are, we will be’

“We were, we are, we will be. Happy birthday, Hungary!” opposition Fidesz leader Viktor Orbán said in a post on Facebook on Thursday to mark the 20 August national holiday. In his post, the former prime minister shared a music video for the song Megmaradni magyarnak (To Remain Hungarian) by the band Kiss Kata, commenting: “It’s a beautiful song, thank you!”

Meanwhile, János Bóka, Fidesz’s parliamentary group leader, pledged to uphold Hungary’s cross-border community, the family, sovereignty, and a self-sustaining economy, and to resist “autocracy” and the “selling out of the country”. “St Stephen’s work holds timeless lessons,” Bóka said in a video posted on Facebook, marking the national holiday. “I believe that our cross-border community is an asset which survived the 20th century and must be preserved in the 21st century as well.”

He called for resistance against “autocracy”, defence of Hungarian families and values, and solidarity with Hungarians beyond the borders. “We must distinguish truth from falsehood, appearance from reality… Hungary and its people can count on us,” he said. Bóka stressed that Hungary’s fate is tied to Christian Europe, where its peace and prosperity must be secured.

World.title: Why is 20 August Hungary’s national holiday? Here is what Hungarians celebrate
World.content:
20 August is one of Hungary’s most important national holidays. Known as St Stephen’s Day and the Day of the Foundation of the State, it honours Hungary’s first king, St Stephen I, and the establishment of the medieval Hungarian Christian state. The public holiday is marked across the country with concerts, cultural programmes, traditional celebrations and spectacular fireworks. But why exactly is 20 August so important to Hungarians?

St Stephen, the founder of the Hungarian state

To understand 20 August, we have to go back more than 1,000 years to the reign of Stephen I, the first king of Hungary.

Stephen was born around 970–975, probably in Esztergom, and succeeded his father, Grand Prince Géza, in 997. At the time, the Hungarian principality was undergoing a major transformation. Stephen continued the process of integrating Hungary into Christian Europe, establishing a centralised kingdom and introducing institutions that would shape the country for centuries.

He supported the spread of Christianity, established dioceses and organised the Hungarian Church, while replacing much of the old tribal political structure with a system of royal administration. The kingdom was divided into counties, or vármegyék, which became the basic units of royal government.

Stephen was crowned king around the turn of the millennium. His reign is generally regarded as the foundation of the Hungarian Christian state, and his efforts to consolidate the kingdom earned him a lasting place in Hungarian history.

King Stephen’s equestrian statue in the Buda Castle. Photo: depositphotos.com

Why do Hungarians celebrate on 20 August?

The date itself is connected not to Stephen’s coronation or death, but to his canonisation. King Stephen died in 1038 and was buried in Székesfehérvár. In 1083, during the reign of King Ladislaus I, Stephen was canonised along with his son, Prince Emeric. The ceremony took place on 20 August, which subsequently became associated with the saintly king.

Over the centuries, St Stephen became much more than a medieval monarch. He came to symbolise Hungarian statehood, Christianity and the continuity of the Hungarian nation. The celebration has therefore had both religious and national significance for centuries.

From a religious feast to a national holiday

The history of 20 August is almost as complicated as Hungary’s own history. The day was recognised as a public holiday under Habsburg rule, and in 1891 it was formally made a non-working day. By then, St Stephen’s Day had become an important expression of Hungarian national identity.

The holiday’s meaning changed dramatically after the Second World War. Under the communist regime, the authorities sought to remove its religious and historical associations. In 1949, the new Stalinist constitution was proclaimed on 20 August, and the day was subsequently celebrated as Constitution Day.

The traditional meaning of the holiday returned after the political transition of 1989–90. Today, Hungary’s Fundamental Law explicitly defines 20 August as the official state holiday, commemorating both the foundation of the state and King St Stephen, the founder of the state.

The Holy Right and one of Hungary’s most famous traditions

One of the most recognisable religious traditions connected to the day is the procession of the Holy Right (Szent Jobb), the mummified right hand traditionally believed to belong to St Stephen.

The relic is preserved at St Stephen’s Basilica in Budapest and is carried in a ceremonial procession on 20 August. The tradition reflects the close connection between the saintly king, Hungarian Christianity and the national holiday.

Another long-standing element of the celebrations is the blessing of the new bread. This tradition connects the holiday not only with statehood and St Stephen, but also with the agricultural year and the harvest.

Why are there fireworks on 20 August?

For many people, especially visitors to Budapest, the most spectacular part of 20 August is the evening fireworks over the Danube.

Large-scale fireworks have become one of the defining images of Hungary’s state holiday, with crowds gathering along the riverbanks and bridges to watch the display. Government-organised celebrations have traditionally combined the fireworks with concerts, family programmes, military ceremonies and other cultural events.

However, the celebrations are by no means limited to Budapest. Events are held throughout Hungary, from village festivals and folk programmes to concerts and major cultural events. The famous Debrecen Flower Carnival, for example, is traditionally held around 20 August and has become one of the country’s best-known celebrations.

20 August today: a celebration of Hungary’s past and present

For Hungarians, 20 August is about much more than fireworks. It is a day commemorating the establishment of a Hungarian state more than a thousand years ago, the legacy of St Stephen and the country’s Christian heritage. At the same time, the holiday has accumulated traditions from very different periods of Hungarian history, from the blessing of the new bread to modern concerts and spectacular Danube fireworks.

It is also an official public holiday, meaning many shops, offices and other services operate differently than on a normal weekday. For visitors in Hungary, this can mean an unusual atmosphere: streets and public spaces become lively with celebrations, while some businesses and services close or operate on holiday schedules.

So, if you happen to be in Hungary on 20 August, don’t be surprised if you see Hungarian flags everywhere, hear live music in public squares or find crowds gathering along the Danube in Budapest. You are witnessing one of the country’s most important celebrations — a holiday whose roots reach back more than 1,000 years.

World.title: Former Orbán ministers launch surprising initiative, Fidesz members are not happy about it
World.content:
Former government minister Tibor Navracsics and former space research commissioner Orsolya Ferencz have launched a new civic initiative calling for dialogue about Hungary’s future and an assessment of the lessons of the past 36 years.

Announced on 20 August, the Civic Democrats (Polgári Demokraták) initiative aims to bring together people regardless of their party affiliation or political worldview. The announcement comes after a period of political upheaval in Hungary and growing criticism within the former governing camp over its response to defeat at the April election.

Navracsics: Hungary needs a way beyond the two sides

In a video published on the national holiday, Navracsics said Hungary had reached a point where the “extreme and destructive confrontation between two sides” was damaging the country’s unity and ability to act. He argued that a new dialogue was needed to move beyond the entrenched political divide.

“Instead of two sides, we need a straight path,”

Navracsics said, describing himself and Ferencz as “civic democrats”, he invited people from across the political spectrum to take part in meetings and discussions about Hungary’s future.

The initiative is intended to examine the lessons of the past 100 days, the past 16 years and the past 36 years, Navracsics said, with the aim of finding solutions that could help create a Hungary that is “homely, liveable and happy”.

He also argued that political revenge and excluding opponents from the political community lead nowhere. Even when people disagree peacefully, he said, they should remain members of the same democratic political community.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

Ferencz calls for a calmer political culture

Ferencz, who served as Hungary’s space research commissioner and was previously a Fidesz MP, also shared the announcement on Facebook. She said Hungarian public life needed honesty, value-based institution-building, calm and civilised conversations, constructive debate and a level-headed assessment without taboos.

Ferencz called for an end to what she described as the “camp mentality” that has come to dominate Hungarian politics, arguing that genuine social dialogue requires moving beyond rigid political camps.

Her comments follow earlier criticism of the former governing side after the April election, in which Fidesz-KDNP suffered defeat and the Tisza Party secured a two-thirds majority. Both Navracsics and Ferencz have previously discussed the need for renewal on the right and for a political community representing the ideal of a civic Hungary.

The initiative creates tension with the Fidesz leadership, with fierce-sounding reactions

The announcement has already prompted a response from Fidesz’s communications director Bertalan Havasi. Speaking to the Hungarian state news agency MTI, Havasi said Fidesz itself currently had no official position on Navracsics’s initiative, but added that he personally did.

“As a civic democrat, the straight path for me is Fidesz,” Havasi said, while arguing that confrontation with the Tisza Party was necessary and should be strengthened. He also said that dialogue with Péter Magyar, the leader of the Tisza Party, was impossible. Havasi added that the “resistance declaration” adopted by Fidesz’s national leadership and parliamentary group in July remained in force.

The declaration described Hungary’s new political system as illegitimate and accused the government of establishing it through a serious violation of the constitution with the aim of obtaining exclusive control of power. Fidesz said it rejected what it called the new “authoritarian system” and would not participate in the appointment of people replacing removed office-holders.

Bertalan Havasi delivering a speech on 9 July. Screenshot: Hír TV/YouTube

Navracsics has increasingly questioned Fidesz’s direction

The new initiative comes after months in which Navracsics has taken a more critical position towards his former political camp. In July, he questioned whether the Fidesz brand could still be saved and shared Ferencz’s call for a new political community based on the ideal of a civic Hungary.

In an earlier interview, Navracsics said efforts were initially focused on mobilising energy within the party, but suggested that a new political force could become necessary if Fidesz were to break apart. Ferencz has likewise criticised the former governing side for failing to adequately confront the reasons for its electoral defeat and renew itself.

Navracsics remains involved in Fidesz-related political work and became head of the party’s municipal affairs cabinet. He also addressed Fidesz’s June leadership congress, where Viktor Orbán was re-elected as party chairman for another year.

Stay up-to-date: Former Fidesz minister János Lázár gives up his seat in Parliament, with one warning to his party

A new political force or a forum for dialogue?

For now, it remains unclear whether the Civic Democrats initiative will develop into a formal political organisation or remain a broader civic platform.

Navracsics has presented it primarily as a space for dialogue rather than conventional party politics. Its immediate focus appears to be bringing together people who may disagree politically but are willing to discuss Hungary’s future outside the increasingly polarised framework of the country’s two main political camps.

The response from Fidesz, however, suggests that even an initiative explicitly designed to move beyond political confrontation may struggle to escape Hungary’s deeply divided political landscape.

The coming months could therefore reveal whether the Civic Democrats can establish a genuinely independent forum for discussion — or whether Navracsics and Ferencz’s initiative becomes part of the wider realignment taking place on the Hungarian right.

World.title: Breaking: Former Fidesz minister János Lázár gives up his seat in Parliament, with one warning to his party – update: Fidesz, Magyar
World.content:
János Lázár, a former minister in Hungary’s previous government and arguably Fidesz’s most prominent political figure after Viktor Orbán, has resigned from his parliamentary mandate, effective 20 August.

Former transport minister leaves Parliament

Lázár announced the decision in a lengthy Facebook post on Thursday, saying he had originally committed to serving in the Fidesz parliamentary group for no more than one year. He had planned to return his mandate to the community that had entrusted it to him.

He said he had initially supported remaining in Parliament because he agreed with the party leadership that Fidesz needed both renewal and political continuity. Following the party’s defeat at the 2026 election, however, he said his view had changed. “The renewal of the party is more important today than representing continuity,” Lázár wrote.

Lázár accepts responsibility for Fidesz’s defeat

The former minister identified three main reasons for his resignation, the first being responsibility. He argued that Fidesz’s electoral defeat was the result of a failure to adapt, combined with personal and institutional hubris. According to Lázár, the party confused its long period in power with invincibility and the absence of a serious challenger with infallibility.

He acknowledged that the party had responded too late and too weakly to allegations of corruption and lavish lifestyles. At the same time, he said Fidesz had failed to adequately counter what he described as a smear campaign against its politicians. “We did not refute the lies, we did not protect each other or ourselves against unfounded accusations,” he wrote.

Lázár also accepted personal responsibility, saying he had made statements that harmed Fidesz and, in some cases, himself. He added that his “Lázár Info” meetings had taught him a great deal about Hungarian voters, governing and his own political role. Most importantly, he said, direct feedback from voters should be the most important point of reference in politics.

He accuses the Tisza government of building an “authoritarian” system

Lázár’s second reason for resigning was what he called “arbitrariness”. He accused the Tisza government led by Péter Magyar of deciding who could stand in elections and who could not, and argued that the government’s first 100 days had shown the direction in which the new political system was moving.

Lázár claimed that Magyar was seeking scapegoats rather than solutions and accused the government of pursuing political opponents through what he described as disenfranchisement, false accusations, unfounded complaints, politically motivated prosecutions and political retaliation.

He argued that Magyar’s priority was not raising Hungary’s position but destroying Fidesz, warning that a politics driven by revenge could push the country towards chaos. These are Lázár’s political accusations and were not independently substantiated in the material provided.

“The party needs real renewal”

His third reason was renewal. Lázár said he considered himself a constructive politician who sought cooperation, and argued that he no longer had a place in what he described as parliamentary “circus” and daily personal political battles. He said he was not attempting to evade political responsibility, but would instead hand his political opportunity entirely to the successor chosen by Fidesz.

For Lázár, however, replacing individual politicians is only a means rather than the goal of renewal. He called for a substantive political transformation within Fidesz, including changes to the party’s organisation and culture, as well as “a new direction and new leadership”. He argued that the party must consistently represent its political identity without contradictions or compromises, while also adapting its internal structures to the new political environment.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

A 25-year parliamentary career comes to an end

Lázár’s resignation closes a 25-year chapter of parliamentary politics. At 51, he stressed that he still has the energy, experience and desire to work, and said he wanted to learn new things and take on new challenges. “The renewal so often spoken about must begin not only in politics and in the party, but within ourselves as well,” he wrote. “That is what I am doing.”

His departure follows weeks in which Lázár had reportedly been assessing the condition of Fidesz’s organisation across Hungary. He travelled around the country at the party leadership’s request to gauge the state of its local and regional organisations following the election defeat.

Stay up-to-date: Hungary’s revamped public broadcaster launches new flagship news bulletin with a surprising shift

Biggest Fidesz figures voluntarily leave the limelight

His resignation also further changes the composition of Fidesz’s former political leadership. Of the three prominent Fidesz figures who were central to the 2026 campaign — Viktor Orbán, Péter Szijjártó and Lázár himself — none will now be a member of Parliament.

Lázár’s decision therefore represents more than the end of his parliamentary career. His own explanation presents it as a deliberate contribution to Fidesz’s renewal at a moment when the party is being forced to reconsider both its political strategy and its organisation after its electoral defeat.

Read also: Hungary celebrates 20 August, PM Magyar sends unusual message to military, air parade over Budapest — Video

UPDATE: Fidesz reaction

According to Fidesz’s statement published after Lázár’s resignation, the former minister’s decision is “part of the planned restructuring of the Fidesz parliamentary group. We thank him for his work as a member of parliament on behalf of Hungary and the Hungarian people. We will provide information in due course regarding the filling of the vacant seat and the next steps in the restructuring process,” they wrote.

Magyar’s reaction: Classic example of a sinking ship

In a speech delivered at the national gathering of the Tisza Islands (Tisza Szigetek) on Margaret Island, Péter Magyar responded to János Lázár’s resignation from his parliamentary seat. Magyar briefly touched on János Lázár in his speech. “This is a classic case of a sinking ship,” he said, after noting that he had read the news on his way to the stage, Telex writes.

World.title: Hungary’s revamped public broadcaster launches new flagship news bulletin with a surprising shift
World.content:
Hungary’s public broadcaster has launched its revamped flagship news programme, with its first edition featuring comments from opposition figures and critics of the government: a notable change in tone following a major overhaul of the public media’s news operation.

The new Híradó aired for the first time at 6 AM on 20 August, Hungary’s national holiday, with presenter Máté Kis at the helm. The programme returned to the air after news services on M1 were suspended on 7 July, when several public media channels temporarily went off air.

Opposition views featured in first broadcast

The first story focused on newly elected President András Baka taking office. Alongside members of the government, the report featured Gábor Horn, chairman of the board of trustees of the Republikon Foundation.

The programme also presented the positions of opposition parties, Fidesz and Mi Hazánk, on Baka’s election, Telex writes.

Critical voices were included in several subsequent reports as well. One segment covered an interactive map published by the Prime Minister’s Office showing government support received by civil organisations. The report also included a post by Péter Takács, a former state secretary for health who has been critical of the government.

The revamped Híradó also reported on the public broadcaster itself. Viewers were told that the public media organisation had terminated all contracts with companies owned by businessman Gyula Balásy, while another report covered the candidates for the newly established Independent Public Media Council. The programme noted that professional organisations had criticised the selection process.

Another report featured Kata Janecskó, a journalist with investigative outlet Direkt36, discussing previously undisclosed child protection reports obtained by the organisation following legal proceedings.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

New faces and a retro-inspired sports bulletin

According to the programme credits, the new Híradó is directed by István Lakatos, while its editor is Balázs Bodacz, the temporary head of the news directorate. The first edition was followed by the new TeleSport sports bulletin, whose visual design deliberately evokes the classic look of the programme from the 1990s.

Weather presenter Tamás Tóth, who previously worked in the same role for the public broadcaster, then delivered the weather forecast. The noon edition of Híradó will be presented by Szimonetta Mészáros, a former member of the Nemzeti Sportrádió and Petőfi Rádió teams.

From 21 August, the public broadcaster is scheduled to air two editions of Híradó each day, at noon and 7.30 PM. On 20 August, however, four editions are scheduled, at 6 AM, noon, 7.30 PM and 10 PM.

Who is the new Híradó presenter?

The broadcaster has also introduced Máté Kis, who presented the first edition. Kis graduated from the University of Szeged with a degree in economics specialising in tourism. He began working in television while still a university student, joining Szeged Television as a reporter in 2020. He later became an anchor on the channel’s news programme before moving to the revamped public media Híradó.

Sport has also played an important role in his life: he previously competed in canoeing and has also worked as a football referee.

If you missed it: New chapter may begin in history of public service media on 20 August

Public media overhaul under scrutiny

The launch comes amid a broader restructuring of Hungary’s public media operation. Before the new Híradó went on air, reports emerged that some members of the previous M1 team would remain in their positions, including staff who had worked on material criticised as government propaganda.

Bodacz subsequently rejected the suggestion that members of the old team had been involved in preparing the 20 August broadcast. He said on Telex’s Facebook page that none of the presenters or reporters working on the first edition had previously worked for M1 in their respective roles, while the former deputy operational news director had also left his position.

The revamped news operation is therefore facing close scrutiny as viewers assess whether the changes represent a genuine editorial transformation of Hungary’s public media — or primarily a change in presentation and personnel.

The first Híradó also formed part of a 20 August broadcast schedule led by Antónia Mészáros and Ádám Bősze, who returned to the public broadcaster’s screens for the national holiday.

During the subsequent festive programming, Bősze described the day as the beginning of the public media’s renewal. The programme also featured teacher and influencer József Balatoni, known as “Jocó bácsi”, and physicist and influencer Janka Sára Molnár. AI-generated visuals were also used for some of the programme’s transitions and background images.

World.title: Hungary celebrates 20 August, PM Magyar sends unusual message to military, air parade over Budapest — Video
World.content:
Hungary marked its national day on Thursday with a traditional flag-raising and military commissioning ceremony in front of Parliament, as Prime Minister Péter Magyar called on newly sworn officers to remain loyal to Hungary rather than any government or political party.

This year’s 20 August marks Hungary’s 1026 years

The 20 August celebrations, held in Budapest’s Kossuth Square, commemorate the foundation of the Hungarian state and Saint Stephen, Hungary’s first king. The day began with the ceremonial raising of the national flag with full military honours, attended by President András Baka, Prime Minister Péter Magyar and Speaker of Parliament Ágnes Forsthoffer.

The Hungarian Defence Forces’ ceremonial unit raised the flag to the national anthem, accompanied by the central military band and the national mounted ceremonial unit. Government and military officials, members of the diplomatic corps and hundreds of spectators also attended. The flag-raising was followed by the swearing-in and commissioning of newly qualified military officers.

Magyar: building a country takes generations

Addressing the newly commissioned lieutenants, Magyar said Saint Stephen understood that establishing a country was not the result of a single decision, battle or law, but of “years, decades and centuries of persistent work”.

He said the officers’ oath might take only a few moments to recite, while the preparation behind it takes years. Early mornings, repeated exercises, examinations, training and exhaustion are largely invisible from the outside, he noted.

“The preparation takes place in peace; its significance becomes clear in times of trouble,” the prime minister said. Magyar also reflected on Hungary’s military history, describing it as a centuries-old and often painful story containing both victories and defeats. He noted that Hungarian soldiers had at times been forced to bear the consequences of decisions they had not made themselves.

Péter Magyar delivering his speech at Kossuth Square. Photo: MTI/Bruzák Noémi

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

A modern military must defend more than borders

According to Magyar, the role of the Hungarian military has changed significantly since the eras of military figures such as Artúr Görgei, György Klapka and János Damjanich. Modern threats are no longer confined to a country’s borders. Cyber systems, energy supplies, transport networks, communications and other critical infrastructure can also be targeted, he said.

Defending the country therefore requires not only military strength but also technological expertise and the ability to respond rapidly to unexpected situations.

Magyar pointed to the recent deployment of the armed forces at the Paks nuclear power plant amid exceptionally low water levels on the Danube. He said soldiers were still working there not for ceremonial purposes or publicity, but because the country needed them.

He stressed that military service can involve much more than carrying weapons. Soldiers may also build bridges and flood defences, deliver water or help ensure the supply of communities during emergencies. The prime minister said he hoped the greatest achievement of the new generation of officers would be never having to fight a war.

“Serve Hungary, not a political side”

One of the strongest messages in Magyar’s speech concerned the political neutrality of the armed forces. He told the officers that, in a functioning country, a soldier should serve the homeland rather than a political side. Governments come and go, he said, but Hungary remains.

Consequently, the military oath is not an oath to a government, prime minister or political party, but to Hungary and the Hungarian people.

“Do not always agree with me,” Magyar told the newly commissioned officers, asking instead that they become good and loyal soldiers of the country, good professionals, law-abiding members of the armed forces and protectors of the people.

He added that if they ever faced a moment when a difficult decision had to be made, Hungary’s interests should come first. A strong country, he argued, needs strong institutions rather than merely obedient ones, and strong institutions require people of strong character.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar delivering his speech on 20 August at Kossuth Square. Photo: MTI/Bruzák Noémi

Defence minister highlights duty and sacrifice

Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi also addressed the officers before their oath. He said the words of a military oath do not become important on the day they are spoken, but when keeping them becomes difficult.

Ruszin-Szendi highlighted the work of Hungarian troops in a range of situations, from the response at Paks and firefighting and water distribution to international missions in the Balkans and North Africa.

Military service, he stressed, can require significant personal sacrifice because soldiers must also be prepared for unexpected situations. He also noted that he could not remember the last time a prime minister had addressed the nation’s armed forces at the state ceremony.

Climate resilience also features in 20 August message

The national day was also used to address Hungary’s broader challenges. Budapest Mayor Gergely Karácsony said Hungary was facing increasingly severe heat, drought and water-related risks. He described the unusually low level of the Danube and the summer’s extreme heat and drought as signs that climate change is already affecting everyday life.

Karácsony argued that extreme heat, prolonged drought and sudden flooding could increasingly become the new normal, with consequences for agriculture, housing, transport, health and social conditions.

He called for continuous adaptation and stronger resilience across Hungary, particularly in Budapest, and said green policy should be viewed not simply as an ideology but as a practical response to the challenges posed by climate change.

Viktor Orbán posted a short message on social media

Meanwhile, former prime minister and Fidesz leader Viktor Orbán marked the national holiday on Facebook with a short video and a brief message: “We were, we are, we will be. Happy birthday, Hungary.”

The different messages nevertheless shared a common theme: 20 August remains a day centred on the endurance, protection and future of the Hungarian state — and on the people expected to carry that responsibility into the next generation.

World.title: New analysis: Hungary’s government is full steam ahead with adopting the euro
World.content:
Hungary’s new government says it has inherited a significantly worse fiscal position than expected, but argues that its first months in office already point to a change in direction. With the government targeting euro adoption by 2030, reducing the budget deficit and public debt is to become one of the defining economic challenges of the coming years.

From a 3.7 per cent target to an 8.3 per cent warning

The 2026 budget was originally approved with a deficit target of around 3.7 per cent of GDP. According to the new government’s review, however, the deficit could have reached approximately 8.3 per cent without corrective measures. The Finance Ministry now expects the deficit to be around 7.5 per cent of GDP, while MBH Analysis Centre forecasts a slightly more favourable figure of about 7 per cent.

The government says EU funds and other measures have helped prevent the situation from deteriorating further. The budget review also identified additional pressures, including higher local government, road development and healthcare spending, as well as EU recovery funds previously included in calculations but ultimately inaccessible.

At the same time, stronger forint exchange rates, lower yields and the recovery of EU funding have helped improve the fiscal outlook. The government plans to amend the 2026 budget and set a new deficit target by the end of August. A 2027 budget and medium-term fiscal plan are expected by the end of October.

Your story. Your perspective. Our readers. Write for Daily News Hungary!

The deficit could fall substantially in 2027

There are several reasons to expect the deficit to decline next year. Some exceptional expenditures weighing on the 2026 balance will disappear. The so-called “weapon money” payment, for example, is expected to worsen this year’s deficit by roughly half a percentage point of GDP, as reported by Index.

Interest costs could also fall faster than previously anticipated. Lower government bond yields and potential interest-rate cuts would reduce the cost of servicing Hungary’s debt, providing another boost to the budget. Recent figures have offered an early sign of improvement. Finance Minister Kármán András reported a HUF 524 billion (EUR 1.44 billion) budget surplus in July and highlighted a significant reduction in the deficit.

However, he also warned against drawing premature conclusions. Some of July’s improvement resulted from lower-than-planned spending, and certain payments may simply have been postponed rather than eliminated. The real test will therefore be whether fiscal discipline remains in place once these temporary effects disappear.

The 2030 euro target raises the stakes

The government’s ambition to introduce the euro in 2030 gives the fiscal debate a longer-term dimension. If Hungary is to meet the conditions for euro adoption, it will need sustained progress on its deficit and public debt. A single year of improvement will not be enough; the country would need a credible, multi-year fiscal trajectory.

This is why analysts argue that a predictable consolidation plan could be more valuable than a dramatic one-year deficit reduction. Temporary spending cuts or one-off revenues might improve the headline figure, but would not necessarily resolve the underlying structural problem.

A realistic multi-year programme would show investors, businesses and credit-rating agencies how the government intends to reduce the deficit and debt while maintaining economic stability.

Stay up-to-date: Central bank claims meeting euro adoption criteria would benefit Hungary’s entire economy

Wider economic challenges remain

Fiscal consolidation alone will not solve Hungary’s broader economic problems. MBH analysts point to weak external demand, particularly subdued German industrial performance, as a continuing risk. Hungary’s dependence on imported energy also leaves the economy exposed to international oil and gas prices, while geopolitical tensions could add further pressure.

Tax and competitiveness measures, investment decisions and expectations surrounding possible euro adoption will therefore also influence Hungary’s growth prospects. For now, the government can point to early signs of fiscal improvement. But the decisive question is whether these developments mark a lasting change rather than a temporary adjustment.

If the 2030 euro ambition is to become more than a political target, Hungary will need years of consistent fiscal discipline, steadily falling deficits and a credible path for reducing public debt.

World.title: The Sziget Festival at a crossroads: can one of Europe’s biggest festivals be revived?
World.content:
Sziget Festival has survived ownership changes, a pandemic and more than three decades of transformation. But after a financially disappointing 2026 edition, the Budapest event faces perhaps a more fundamental question: what should Sziget actually be in the years ahead?

There is something unusual about discussing the future of Sziget Festival in terms of survival. For decades, the event seemed almost permanent: every August, a corner of Budapest was transformed into a temporary international city, populated by music fans from across Europe and far beyond.

Yet the numbers from 2026 make uncomfortable reading.

According to Economx, this year’s festival attracted around 350,000–360,000 visits, considerably below the organisers’ target of 400,000 and down from approximately 416,000 the previous year. The financial result was also worse than planned.

Last year’s loss was around HUF 2.8 billion (approximately EUR 7.7 million), while the aim for 2026 had been to reduce the deficit to HUF 1.5 billion (around EUR 4.1 million). That target was not achieved.

Why Sziget Festival is struggling

The reasons go beyond whether this year’s line-up was strong enough.

Founder Károly Gerendai, who returned to the business after the departure of foreign owner Superstruct Entertainment, pointed to a four-month delay in preparations and ticket sales. That mattered because historically almost a third of passes had been sold during this early sales period.

International demand also weakened. A stronger Hungarian forint made Budapest more expensive for overseas visitors, while higher travel costs and geopolitical conflicts affected several important markets, including the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Israel and Ukraine. Meanwhile, Hungarians accounted for 53% of the 2026 audience.

There is an uncomfortable truth behind these figures. Sziget can no longer rely on being the inexpensive Central European alternative to Western festivals.

Gerendai acknowledged that the enormous price advantage Sziget enjoyed 10 or 20 years ago has diminished. He nevertheless argued that visitors still receive relatively good value because a Sziget pass covers considerably more festival days and programmes than many similarly priced European events.

From Student Island to the Island of Freedom

For international readers, it is worth remembering how far Sziget has travelled.

The festival began in 1993 as Diáksziget, or Student Island, created by Gerendai, musician Péter Müller Sziámi and their collaborators on Óbuda Island in the Danube. The first edition attracted around 43,000 paying visitors and was primarily a Hungarian cultural gathering rather than an international pop spectacle.

It gradually became one of Europe’s largest music and cultural festivals. International stars arrived, visitor numbers multiplied and the event developed its distinctive “Island of Freedom” identity. Crucially, Sziget was never supposed to be only a row of large concerts: theatre, circus, world music, art, community programmes and encounters between nationalities became part of its appeal. The festival itself says visitors from more than 100 nationalities now attend.

That history matters because it may also contain the answer to Sziget’s present difficulties.

The future may depend on becoming more Sziget, not less

Gerendai believes the model built primarily around an impressive list of headliners is no longer sufficient. Instead, the festival’s future could depend on cultural diversity, community experiences and something its competitors cannot easily reproduce: Budapest itself.

As he told Pénzcentrum, few festivals of this scale take place inside a major European capital. Sziget visitors can spend the afternoon exploring Budapest and return to the island for the evening. Turning the festival and the city into one combined travel experience could therefore become one of its strongest international selling points.

That argument feels particularly convincing. Sziget is unlikely to win a permanent bidding war for every superstar against the world’s richest promoters. But no rival can copy Budapest, the Danube or the strange experience of stepping out of an ordinary European capital and into a temporary festival city.

The operational picture is also less bleak than the financial headlines suggest. Pénzcentrum reported that consumer protection authorities inspected nearly 120 catering outlets during the festival. The overall findings were favourable, with most businesses complying with legal and food-safety requirements and minor problems generally corrected quickly. As we wrote earlier, Sziget attendance plunges as founder warns festival must “move forward to break free”

Foreign visitors show why Sziget matters beyond the festival gates

The economic importance of international visitors becomes particularly clear in new figures published after this year’s Sziget Festival. According to a GKI survey of 529 festivalgoers, an average foreign visitor spent HUF 255,000 (around EUR 700) during their trip, compared with HUF 108,000 (around EUR 296) for a Hungarian guest. Even after subtracting the roughly HUF 95,000 (EUR 260) that foreign visitors spent on travel, their expenditure remained substantially higher. Perhaps just as importantly for Sziget’s positioning, only 28% of foreign respondents considered the festival expensive, while 11% actually regarded its prices as low.

If you missed it: Sziget Festival 2026 in numbers: foreigners vs Hungarians, unsatisfied organisers, the festival’s future

The impact also extends well beyond Óbuda Island. Among respondents who do not live in Budapest, 83% spent at least one additional day in the capital or its surroundings outside their time at the festival; 29% stayed for another three to five days, while a further 25% remained for more than five. These visitors spent an average HUF 98,000 (around EUR 268) outside Sziget itself. With the festival estimating that around 58,000 foreign guests attended in 2026, their combined spending amounted to roughly HUF 15 billion (about EUR 41 million). That gives Gerendai’s argument about selling Budapest and Sziget as a combined experience a measurable economic dimension: attracting international festivalgoers does not only fill the island, but also hotels, restaurants and other businesses across the capital.

Sziget Festival will return in 2027 – but the real test starts now

There is no immediate farewell on the horizon. Sziget Festival has already confirmed its return in 2027 as a five-day event, August 10-14, 2027.

The full-price Super Early Bird pass has been set at EUR 299, or EUR 318 including the handling fee. Advance registration has already begun, even before the first artists have been announced.

That is both a statement of confidence and a gamble.

The question is no longer simply whether Sziget can attract a bigger headliner next summer. It is whether the festival can convince a new generation that travelling to Budapest for several days offers something that an arena concert, a weekend festival or an endless stream of online entertainment cannot.

Perhaps the way forward is hidden in Sziget’s own past. The festival became important not because it was merely big, but because it felt different. Its future may depend on rediscovering exactly that.

World.title: Romanian government commits EUR 1 bln to develop advanced tech within TechUp program
World.content:
The government approved the TechUp Romania Program on Thursday, August 20. The initiative includes a new financing line worth more than EUR 1 billion, which aims to transform research into production and develop advanced technologies.

The program focuses on areas with high added-value potential such as advanced computing, artificial intelligence, microelectronics and digital infrastructure; biotechnology, Agri-Tech and precision health; green energy, storage and climate technologies; mobility, space and autonomous systems; advanced materials and Industry 4.0; cybersecurity and digital security.

Sizable budget

The total budget of TechUp Romania, which was established at the proposal of the Ministry of Finance, is RON 5.313 billion, of which RON 2.656 billion is allocated to regional investment aid and RON 2.657 billion to research and development projects. The average annual budget is approximately RON 759 million, equivalent to EUR 150 million. Financing agreements may be issued between 2026 and 2032, while payments will be made between 2027 and 2041, according to the official press release.

To be financed, projects submitted under this program must have eligible costs between RON 5 and 50 million and include two successive components: a minimum of RON 2 million for research and development and a minimum of RON 3 million for investment in production or service provision capacity. The two stages involve a single application for a financing agreement.

“With TechUp, for the first time, we are linking research and production in a single financing pathway and introducing the possibility of granting an advance for research. We want to make better use of Romanian human capital, direct it toward entrepreneurship and advanced technologies, and keep intellectual property within the company that develops the technology,” said interim finance minister Alexandru Nazare, cited by News.ro.

In the program, the government not only finances research or investment in production capacities, but creates, for the first time, an integrated mechanism that links the two stages and supports the transformation of a technology developed in Romania into a product and a competitive industrial capacity, officials from the Ministry of Finance said.

Tax deductions and grants

One of the main new features of the mechanism is the possibility of granting an advance of up to 30% of the annual value of the approved grant for the research and development component. A new advance application may be submitted after the previous one has been justified, while beneficiaries using this mechanism submit quarterly reports on the project’s progress and use of funds.

For the research and development component, the program combines grants with a 200% tax deduction for certain eligible expenses involving tangible and intangible assets. The maximum aid is 50% for industrial research and 25% for experimental development, to which the regional bonuses provided for by the European framework may be added. For the production stage, support is granted in the form of regional aid, within the limits of the applicable regional aid map.

Beneficiaries

The program involves two categories of beneficiaries. Category A is intended for autonomous enterprises that do not have sufficient resources for their own contribution and that attract private capital from venture capital funds and/or business angels. In this case, the private investor’s involvement also serves as business validation and discipline for projects at a stage when traditional bank financing is difficult to access.

Category B includes enterprises that can secure the necessary contribution from a broader mix of private sources: own capital, reinvested profit, bank loans, intra-group loans, venture capital or business angels.

In both situations, the beneficiary must provide a financial contribution of at least 25% of eligible costs, both for the research and development component and for the production component, from resources that do not benefit from other public support.

TechUp also introduces a more flexible approach for the period following the completion of the investment, the statement noted.

“In the first two years of monitoring, progress toward the market can be demonstrated through a wide range of results: pilot projects with customers, paid tests, letters of intent, purchase interest, progress in certification, customer validation, subsequent financing, intellectual property assets, strategic partnerships or other evidence of progress toward commercialization. The maintenance period may be extended by up to two years if demonstrable progress exists,” according to Finance Ministry officials.

The scheme is designed to take into account the specific nature of investments in DeepTech, where the path from prototype to commercial product is longer and involves a high level of technological and commercial risk. If commercial results fall below initial estimates, the mechanism provides, in certain situations, for proportional recovery according to the degree of underachievement, rather than automatically recovering the entire support.

At the same time, firm conditions remain in place regarding the completion of the research component and reaching the technological maturity level stipulated in the financing agreement.

The Ministry of Finance stated that a central element of the scheme is protecting the technological value created through financing. The beneficiary is required to maintain intellectual property rights over the product or service resulting from the research and development component throughout the entire period of maintaining the investment in production. In addition, the economic activity and intellectual property resulting from the research must be maintained in the region where the investment is carried out for the period stipulated by the scheme.

World.title: Western Romania: Special exhibition in Timișoara to include 69 works by Pablo Picasso
World.content:
69 works by Pablo Picasso from the collection of the Musée Picasso, Antibes, will be on display in Timișoara, between September 17, 2026, and January 17, 2027, in a special exhibition that inaugurates the new Art Encounters space.

The event, titled "Picasso en visite," will include 69 works – paintings, drawings, engravings, lithographs and ceramics.

The exhibition starts from a particular moment in the artist’s life and work.

“In 1946, Picasso received an invitation to work in the spaces of the Grimaldi Castle, at that time the museum of the region’s history and archaeology. The artist had long dreamed of a place where he could work on a different scale than his studio allowed him to. The light of the Mediterranean, the sea, Greek mythology and the atmosphere of southern France became fixed in his imagination during a period of extraordinary creative freedom,” the organizers said in the presentation of the event.

Tickets can be purchased online at bilete.artencounters.ro and through the Entertix platform. To ensure that the visit provides the necessary time and space to encounter the works and for their safety, access to the exhibition is available in time slots and with a limited number of visitors.

Rates:

Adults (18–64 years): RON 65 (Tuesday–Thursday) / 75 (Friday–Sunday)

Children (8–17 years): RON 20 / 25

Family (2 adults + 2 children): RON 150 / 175

Seniors (65+) and students (up to 26 years): RON 35 / 45

Private tour for 2 people: RON 500

Access is free for children under 8 (accompanied by an adult), people with disabilities or reduced mobility and their companions, press representatives and holders of AICA, ICOM and ICOMOS cards.

On the last Tuesday of each month, the exhibition can be visited free of charge, between 10:00 AM and 8:00 PM. Tickets for these days will be available that morning at the Art Encounters ticket office, subject to availability.

During the exhibition, guided tours will be available both in Romanian and in some foreign languages, with prior reservation. Art Encounters will also organize free visits dedicated to school groups, with details about the schedule and registration to be announced soon.

World.title: Romanian meat and ready-made meals processor Cris-Tim reports 34% higher net profit in H1
World.content:
Cris-Tim Family Holding (BVB: CFH), one of the largest players in Romania’s processed meat and ready-made meals market, reported revenues of RON 567.4 million for H1 2026, up 6%, and a net profit of RON 63.6 million, 34% higher compared to the previous year

According to the company, the results were supported by the continued growth of the processed meat segment, which advanced by 7% compared to the previous year.

The Cris-Tim brand remained the main pillar of the segment, generating revenues of RON 348.6 million, up 4% compared to the previous year. The Matache Măcelaru brand recorded revenues advancing by 24% compared to the previous year, to RON 77.8 million, reflecting growing consumer interest in traditional and premium products, as well as the brand’s expanding presence in modern retail networks.

The other brands in the Processed Meat portfolio generated RON 77.2 million, up 9% compared to the previous year, an evolution supported both by the positive dynamics of the company’s brands and by Private Label production. Segment EBITDA reached RON 93.4 million in H1 2026, representing an increase of 28% compared to 2025.

The Ready Meals segment generated revenues of RON 55.7 million in H1 2026, down 2% compared to the previous year, and accounted for approximately 10% of total revenues. Sales volumes decreased by 8% compared to the previous year, while the average selling price per ton increased by 7%, reflecting a more favorable product mix.

The Bunătăți brand generated revenues of RON 34.3 million in H1 2026, compared to RON 35.9 million in H1 2025, while the other brands in the Ready Meals portfolio advanced by 3% compared to the previous year, to RON 21.4 million, an evolution supported by the expanding presence in modern retail networks and the diversification of the product range. Despite the slight decline in segment revenues, Ready Meals EBITDA increased by 11% compared to the previous year, to RON 15.2 million, reflecting the improved sales mix and the stronger contribution of products with higher margins.

Overall EBITDA increased by 28% compared to the previous year, to RON 110.7 million in H1 2026, while the EBITDA margin increased by 3.4 percentage points, to 19.5%, compared to 16.1% in H1 2025.

“The improvement was mainly driven by the favorable procurement strategy, increased production efficiency and an improved product mix. Profit before tax increased by 41% compared to the previous year, to RON 79.8 million, while net profit reached RON 63.6 million, up 34% compared to the previous year, and the net profit margin improved to 11.2%, compared to 8.9% in H1 2025,” the company report stated.

“In just a few months, two of our newest products – Gratarescu and Durdulii, the latter launched under the Matache Măcelaru brand – have quickly become among consumers’ preferred choices in their respective categories,” said Radu Timiș Jr., CEO of Cris-Tim Family Holding, in his message to investors.

As of June 30, 2026, the company's cash position reached RON 139.1 million. Net debt stood at RON 116 million, compared to a net cash position of RON 5.6 million at the end of 2025, mainly reflecting the seasonal accumulation of inventories and investments made in the first half of the year, according to the company. The debt level remained moderate, with the annualized net debt-to-EBITDA ratio standing at 0.52x, and the net debt-to-equity ratio at 29.4%.

Following the H1 2026 results, which exceeded expectations, management updated the 2026 Income and Expenditure Budget. The updated budget reflects significantly higher profitability expectations, with EBITDA currently estimated to reach RON 238 million, approximately 14% above the initially approved budget, and gross profit at RON 173.9 million, approximately 19% above the initial target. The revised EBITDA margin is estimated to reach 19.8%, compared to 17.1% according to the initial budget.

World.title: British-Romanian Chamber of Commerce appoints Felicia Alexandru as Executive Director
World.content:
The British-Romanian Chamber of Commerce (BRCC) announced the appointment of Felicia Alexandru as Executive Director on Tuesday, August 18.

The appointment comes at a time of growing economic relations between the two countries. Bilateral trade in goods and services reached GBP 10.4 billion in the four quarters ending at the end of March 2026, up 5.6% compared to the previous similar period, according to the latest data from the UK Department for Business and Trade.

According to the BRCC press release, Felicia Alexandru’s priorities will include strengthening dialogue between Chamber members, institutions and authorities, developing the Chamber’s program of events and initiatives, and facilitating new opportunities for collaboration, investment and commercial development in the two markets, Romania and the UK.

“We are pleased to have Felicia join us at an important moment for the development of the BRCC and the economic relationship between Romania and the United Kingdom. Her experience in diplomacy, consulting and coordinating complex teams will support the implementation of the strategic direction established by the Board of Directors,” said Robert Uzună, President of the British-Romanian Chamber of Commerce.

“I take on this role with great confidence, at an excellent time for our trade ties. I am joining the valuable BRCC team with a clear desire to bring a new dynamic and to be close to every business leader. My priority is to listen to the needs of members and transform the remarkable expertise within our network into real projects,” said Felicia Alexandru.

Before joining the BRCC, Felicia Alexandru led the Romanian operations of Aperio Intelligence, a British risk management and business intelligence consultancy. Before this position, starting in 2021, she coordinated the company’s due diligence teams in Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca. Between 2008 and 2019, she worked at the British Embassy in Bucharest. Her experience was complemented by coordinating public integrity programs in the non-governmental sector.

Felicia Alexandru holds a degree in political science from the National University of Political Studies and Public Administration in Bucharest and a master’s degree in international relations and European studies from Central European University in Hungary.

(Photo source: brcconline.eu)

World.title: Romanian F-16 destroys maritime drone near Neptun Deep gas platform in the Black Sea
World.content:
A Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed a maritime drone near the Neptun Deep offshore gas platform in the Black Sea on Thursday, August 20, interim defense minister Radu Miruță announced. The operation was ordered to protect several hundred people working at the site and secure the critical infrastructure, he said.

According to minister Miruțǎ, the Coast Guard announced that the maritime drone was detected several hundred meters from work underway at Neptun Deep, in Romania’s exclusive economic zone, around 80 miles east of Constanța. The Defense Ministry later added that the drone was drifting when it was first reported by a commercial vessel at around 6:28 a.m.

“A maritime drone was destroyed by the Romanian Army using the onboard cannon of a Romanian F-16 aircraft a few moments ago, in the area of the Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea,” Radu Miruță wrote on Facebook on Thursday around noon.

A command cell was established at the Ministry of National Defense following the discovery. The ministry requested that NATO transfer operational command of the response to the Romanian military, according to the interim minister.

“Following the analyses carried out and in coordination with the president of Romania, the decision was made to destroy the drone in order to protect the lives of the several hundred people working on the platform and secure the critical infrastructure,” Miruță said.

Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets were scrambled with authorization to open fire. The maritime drone was subsequently destroyed without incident.

“The drone was destroyed safely,” the interim defense minister announced.

According to him, the Romanian authorities contacted Ukraine through a recently established direct communication channel and received official confirmation that the drone was not of Ukrainian origin.

According to the Defense Ministry, a Coast Guard ship carrying a Romanian Navy explosive ordnance disposal team was sent to the area to conduct further checks, while the operation remained ongoing.

President Nicușor Dan also reacted to the news, saying, "I congratulate the Romanian Armed Forces and the pilots of the two Romanian F-16 fighter jets on the successful mission to destroy the maritime drone near the Neptun Deep platform in the Black Sea. I also congratulate the Coast Guard for promptly reporting the drone’s presence in the area. It was a race-against-time operation in which the highest priority was protecting the lives of those working on the platform and keeping critical infrastructure safe from any potential danger."

"I strongly condemn the intensification of these irresponsible incidents by the Russian Federation. We remain vigilant alongside our NATO allies to defend ourselves and repel such provocations," he added.

This was the first time Romanian aircraft used their onboard cannons and also the first time they engaged a maritime drone, Biziday.ro noted.

The incident came hours after an aerial drone entered Romanian airspace near Galați early on Thursday and crashed in an unpopulated area near Grindu, Tulcea County. Two Spanish F-18 aircraft and a Romanian IAR-330 SOCAT helicopter were deployed during that incident, while residents in the affected area received an RO-Alert warning.

Last week, two Gerbera-type drones were destroyed by divers of the Romanian Army in the exclusive economic zone, approximately 90 nautical miles (around 165 kilometers) from Constanța, in the Neptun Deep exploitation area.
