World.title: Wildlife advocates warn bird flu mass mortality events are a sign of things to come
World.content:
Environmental campaigners are warning the escalation of the nation's H5 bird flu outbreak is a sign of what's to come, after South Australia detected three mass mortality events believed to be linked to the infection.

On the same day SA authorities revealed the death of more than 1,000 crested terns in three separate events, Tasmania also confirmed the loss of more than two dozen penguins and three crested terns.

Testing is still required to confirm bird flu as the cause of the deaths in both states, but authorities believe that to be reason in a clear sign of the growing severity of the outbreak.

The Invasive Species Council said it was "shocking" and "dreaded news".

"It is only the start of the scale of deaths we can expect in the months ahead as the virus spreads," chief executive Jack Gough said.

"The devastation from bird flu is becoming very real."

A dead bird believed to be impacted by bird flu. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

He said Australia might soon face a similar reality to the bird flu outbreak in South America.

"We look at South America, where we're talking hundreds of thousands of birds dead in the first few months and that's the scale of death that we can start to expect," Mr Gough said.

Jack Gough says more needs to be done to protect birds amid the crisis. (Supplied: Invasive Species Council)

"While a thousand birds sounds shocking, this is only the tip of the iceberg in terms if the level of devastation we're going to see and it's going to start becoming very real for people on coastlines around Australia and islands around Australia."

Mr Gough said this could include inland, particularly around wetlands, where birds congregated.

"Australian wildlife needs a bail out, it's facing a huge threat in the form of bird flu, one that we can't stop just as we weren't able to stop the algal bloom in South Australia or the black summer bushfires on the east coast," he said.

"This could be worse than both of those incidents in terms of wildlife impact, and it is going to be very visible and increasingly visible around the whole country."

He said a focus on protecting wildlife areas from other threats including cats, foxes and the destruction of habitat was also crucial.

"That is what is going to be key to how wildlife survive and hopefully are able to thrive in the future after what's going to be a pretty devastating wave of destruction," he said.

Testing is currently being carried out on birds from King Island in Tasmania. (Supplied: Mel Wells )

Will vaccination be effective?

Last week, Victoria announced it would vaccinate 5,000 penguins on Phillip Island, after a bird from the island's colony was found to have died from H5N1 bird flu.

In response to the mass mortality, SA's state Premier Peter Malinauskus yesterday said it would now consider a potential vaccination program "under certain circumstances for certain species", including penguins.

Mr Gough said while vaccination was important, it was also not an easy solution to combat the issue.

Victorian authorities are hoping to vaccinate at least 5,000 little penguins. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

"It's something that potentially in limited circumstances, for some highly restricted species, ones in captivity or ones that are very easy to access can make a difference," he said.

Wildlife Recovery Australia's Chief Executive Officer Dr Stephen Van Mil said vaccination was not a practical solution.

"The reality it's only going to be confined to flightless birds," Mr Van Mil said.

"As far as birds that can fly…you're not going to catch them, not once and definitely not twice."

Dr. Stephen Van Mil says vaccination is not a practical solution. (Bobby Macumber, ABC)

Mr Van Mil said following the mass mortality deaths this week, the organisation had appealed to the federal government to commission more mobile wildlife veterinary hospitals in every state across the country.

"We know how to build them, we can build them quickly, we're just leaning on the federal government to make a decision," Mr Van Mil said.

"We'd be collecting as many live birds as we could and euthanising them and dispose them appropriately, because if dead birds are left exposed, the other birds of prey will come and eat on them and then they will become infected.

"It's really important even though we can't save birds affected by this horrible virus, that we can either humanely euthanise them and or dispose them appropriately."

World.title: Runner breaks national record with 436km over 65 hours
World.content:
Among the lines of dialogue Clint Eastwood set into cinematic immortality is one about everyone having to know their limitations.

For competitors of a recent ultramarathon race named in honour of the Hollywood actor however, those limitations were very ambitious indeed.

In the case of Yuko Sato, they extended to 436 kilometres over the course of 65 hours straight — "course" being something of an operative word.

The runner recently completed that distance by doing laps around a public green space in suburban Brisbane.

Such was the scale of the challenge that it paid to think only a few steps ahead.

"I don't know how I did it," Sato said.

Yuko Sato at the Clint Eastwood Last One Standing at Rocklea over the weekend. (Supplied: Yuko Sato)

What started with ambition ended with something bordering on apparition.

"I was hallucinating. I saw lots of plastic models hanging over the trees, both sides," she said.

"I didn't sleep at all.

"The next day I started to swell in the foot and now I can't fit into any shoes, so probably [for the] next three-to-five days I can't run."

Sato is an ultramarathon runner and competes in a gruelling format called a "backyard ultra".

At the recent race — the Clint Eastwood Last One Standing — at Oxley Creek Common in Rocklea, she set two records, she said — surpassing the Japanese and Australian female runner distance.

An exhausted but proud Yuko Sato breaks the Australian women record for backyard ultra. (Supplied: Yuko Sato)

Backyard ultras work in the following way: competitors have to complete a course of 6.71 kilometres inside an hour. Whatever time they have left over inside the 60 minutes can be used for recuperation — but once that time is up, the runners have to begin the course again.

"We don't know how long it's going to be until we start," Sato said.

"The last one standing is going to win."

In her stride

Born in Japan, Sato moved to Adelaide in 2009 for study. Her pathway into running obeyed no straight track — she started in 2019 after the upheaval of a break-up.

"After the separation I cut off all the connections from the past relationship so, I was alone," she said.

"I joined the running crowd — got to know the people, and then people took me from road running to trail running, and then from trail running to ultra running."

With swollen and exhausted feet, Yuko Sato reflects on her endurance event win. (ABC News: Ashlin Blischeke)

In his memoir "What I Talk About When I Talk About Running", the acclaimed author Haruki Murakami argues that "exerting yourself to the fullest within your individual limits: that's the essence of running".

"Most runners run not because they want to live longer, but because they want to live life to the fullest," the novelist wrote.

"If you're going to while away the years, it's far better to live them with clear goals and fully alive than in a fog, and I believe running helps you do that."

Sato would perhaps agree, and she is keen to point out that while she regards running as competitive, she also finds it collaborative.

"We do compete against each other, but at the same time we're also encouraged to push for each other," she said.

"We [think] we hit the limit — but other runners also take our hands or arms to go one more."

Yuko Sato pushes her limits at this year's Clint Eastwood Last One Standing race. (Supplied: Yuko Sato)

She may be suffering from a swollen foot — but not a swollen ego. Non-stop running, she said, is an experience that keeps you firmly grounded.

"Running's to be humble," she said.

"It's hurting you, but you can see the limit and you can test yourself."

World.title: 'Family is not important?' Australians face uncertain future after visa change
World.content:
Amy Hu was a single mother when she gave birth to her first daughter, so her own mother played an important role in raising the child.

"I'm so very grateful to my mum," Ms Hu said.

"She helped me big time with my daughter."

Ms Hu, a Chinese Australian living in Brisbane, has since remarried and had a son in 2024.

Her mother has again been very helpful, travelling between Australia and China to look after her and the baby.

Every time her temporary visa expired, Ms Hu's mother had to return to China and wait months before reapplying to visit Australia.

Twice she paid for a temporary parent visa which cost more than $6,000 each.

"My daughter was asking me all the time why her grandmother had to leave," Ms Hu said.

Parent visa applicants ageing and dying waiting in decades-long queues Migrant families are putting their lives on hold as they wait years and even decades to hear if their parents will be able to settle in Australia.

In 2019, Ms Hu's mother and father in China both applied for a contributory parent visa, which grants permanent residency for parents of Australian citizens, permanent residents, or eligible New Zealand citizens if the applicant agrees to pay more than $50,000.

A non-contributory visa costs $8,665 but the wait time is much longer.

Ms Hu's parents were expecting to be granted their visas in 2027, but that has become uncertain.

In late July, the Department of Home Affairs introduced a policy prioritising family visa applications lodged onshore over those lodged overseas.

The changes affect not just parents but also other family-stream visas available to partners, children, parents and carers.

Ms Hu started an online petition last week calling on the federal government to treat offshore visa applications fairly.

It has since gained more than 1,600 signatures.

Ms Hu said she felt decision-makers "do not care about the next generation".

"My children are all Australian citizens," she said.

" Am I supposed to tell my children that family is not important? Or grandparents are not important? "

Parents based overseas already face a long wait for their permanent visas to be granted. (AP: Andy Wong)

A Department of Home Affairs spokesperson told the ABC a ministerial direction that came into effect in July supported "targeted delivery of Australia's 2026-27 Family Migration Program, including government's commitment to prioritise applications from onshore migrants".

The spokesperson said changes to the permanent migration program were made "to place downwards pressure on Net Overseas Migration (NOM)".

"Prioritising onshore applicants will help reduce wait times for migrants already living, working, and contributing to Australia," they said.

"Processing of parent visa applications has not paused.

"[The] estimated processing times for the capped migration programs will be updated for 2026-27 in due course."

Before the July policy change, the estimated average processing times for parent visas lodged this year was 15 to 33 years, according to the Home Affairs website.

There are now concerns that wait time could blow out.

Fears wait time could be indefinite

Evon Yu, right, says her mum and dad have already waited for seven years for their visas. (Supplied: Evon Yu)

Evon Yu, one of the signatories of the petition, has also been affected by the policy change.

Ms Yu moved to Sydney as an international student nearly 20 years ago and had been living apart from her parents in China since.

Although she occasionally visits them, she finds it increasingly hard with work and a one-year-old child.

"If they could come and live here, they would definitely help me a lot with child care," she said, adding they would also be an emotional support.

She feared the wait for her parents to join her in Australia could now become indefinite.

Ms Yu said her family was also considering moving back to China if her parents were still waiting for their visas in three to five years' time.

Like Ms Hu's parents, Ms Yu's parents also applied for a contributory parent visa in 2019.

The initial application fee cost more than $8,000, and each applicant needs to pay a second instalment of $43,600 just before they are granted their visa.

'Multi-decade' backlog

Ms Yu said the policy change was just another example of Australia becoming less inclusive.

"I know there are many reasons behind it, but it's really unfair for all family visa applicants overseas," she said.

"It's the parents, in my case. For others, it could be visas for their wives, husbands or children."

Behind the working holiday-makers' visa applications pause Here's what you need to know about the working holiday maker visa applications that are being paused in 24 countries.

An online petition calling for an improved visa processing system with reduced excessive waiting times for partner visas has also gained nearly 1,500 signatures.

Australia has capped permanent family visas at 52,460 for the 2026-27 financial year.

The allocation for parent visas is just 7,060 — the lowest number in a decade, excluding the pandemic period.

The 2023 Review of the Migration System report found there was a "multi-decade" backlog of parent visas and "there have been several unsuccessful attempts to manage this backlog".

According to the report, the number of parent visas have been capped partially due to the cost on taxpayers.

"A skilled migrant has a lifetime positive fiscal benefit of around $200,000," it said.

"A parent, on average, costs $400,000 over their lifetime due to their high use of government-funded services and limited taxes paid."

However, Ms Yu disagreed that parents like hers would be a burden on society.

She said her parents had planned to invest their savings in Australia, which would contribute to the local economy.

"My parents, like many others who applied overseas, they are not that old. They also have decent pension at home, and wouldn't need money from Australia," said Ms Yu, who works in the financial industry.

"I think the economic contribution they might make to Australian society could actually exceed the social costs they incur."

'Families need clarity'

Rajwant Singh, a migration agent, said people who had been sitting in the queue for many years now faced an "uncertain future".

Mr Singh said he believed offshore parent visa applications would still be processed alongside onshore ones, but at a slower speed than before.

Migration Agent Rajwant Singh says affected families need clarity on the new policy. (Supplied)

"Affected families need clarity and reassurance — reassurance that no-one will be treated unfairly."

James Hammond, a migration lawyer, said he did not know how favouring onshore visa applications would impact offshore applicants who already faced long wait times.

Mr Hammond said de-prioritising offshore parent visa applications would not be effective in bringing down net migration numbers.

"The number of visas granted each year in those categories is really a drop in the ocean," he said.

"The fact that people already wait a very long time for those visas, it doesn't really make a lot of sense as far as the government's objective to reduce the overseas migration number is concerned."

Greens senator David Shoebridge said the idea that "immigration systems should be restructured around a short-term reduction of net overseas migration is irresponsible, especially when it means pulling families apart".

He added that the average wait time now for a non-contributory parent visa was 30 years, and 15 years for a contributory visa.

"Last year the devastating reality for over 1,500 families was that they lost their parent while waiting for a visa," he said.

World.title: Rebecca Beeson's remarkable road back to the AFLW
World.content:
There were days Rebecca Beeson could not walk straight, could not watch TV and could not imagine life on the footy field.

Her dream, at that point, was not AFLW glory or a milestone match; it was getting back to feeling normal.

Now, after a journey that has tested her in ways football never could, Beeson is set to run out for her 75th AFLW match as team captain.

And it has been a very long road to get to 75 matches.

The Giants midfielder is the last inaugural GWS player from the first AFLW season in 2017 (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

From three concussions to a season on the sidelines, the 29-year-old said the experience made her the person she is today.

The GWS captain was just a few weeks away from the start of the 2022 season when she suffered a severe head knock in a practice match against Sydney.

It was her third concussion in seven months.

"I didn't immediately know [what had happened]. I knew something wasn't quite right and I needed some time away from the game," Beeson told ABC Sport.

The club doctor and Beeson had a mutual decision to work on her health and to take the seventh AFLW season off.

Amid the uncertainty, the young midfielder was also dealing with her father's sudden death.

"It was one of the most challenging times in my life.

"Initially I was struggling with some delayed concussion symptoms over a number of weeks. I had headaches. I couldn't go for a walk outside because the Sun would make me sick. I couldn't look at my phone," she said.

"I spent a lot of time at home staring at the wall."

Rebecca Beeson suffered two concussions in the 2021 season, then a severe head knock the next year had her sidelined for 12 months. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Dylan Burns)

Specialist after specialist

During her 12-month rehabilitation, Beeson watched her team from the sidelines.

She saw concussion specialist after concussion specialist and travelled to Victoria to see doctors to help her get her quality of life back.

"I did a lot of work with the club's psychologist and a specialist head-injury neuropsychologist down in Melbourne," she said.

"What I found to be scary was just not seeing an endpoint"

Concussion injuries are not only difficult to diagnose because standard brain scans like CT's or MRI's do not show the visible damage, but signs and symptoms of a concussion can vary from person to person.

"I reflect on it, and I obviously would never wish for that to happen to anyone, but I think I came out the other side a better teammate and more grateful to be playing footy," Beeson said.

"It's made me the person that I am today."

Resilient return

Rebecca Beeson was voted the Giants' third captain in the 2024 season after long-time skipper Alicia Eva stepped down. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

Her return to the league in 2023 marked a defining year for the young midfielder: she claimed a second Gabrielle Trainor medal and was named club captain after long-time skipper Alicia Eva stepped down from the role.

Giants coach Cam Bernasconi had only just been appointed when Beeson was injured.

"She's just an incredibly resilient person. Her ability to overcome that and become the leader she is, it's just remarkable," Bernasconi said.

"She spent the 12 months rehabilitating; she brought back neck strengthening and concussion protocol exercises that we now use for the whole playing group.

"As a coach, selfishly, I love that it's her milestone this week because I get to lean on her and use her as motivation for the team," he said.

Over the weekend, the 29-year-old delivered a career-high three goals in round one against West Coast, a performance she will be looking to emulate for her 75th match on Sunday.

"We brought high pressure to the game, and we were the number one pressure team for the comp last week," she said.

"It's a trademark of our game; we want to be known for that, for getting in your face, so that's just something we'll keep working on.

"If I take a step back and think of the journey I've been on, I'm just very happy and very grateful to make it to 75."

World.title: EV sales are surging in Australia. But are they cheaper to run?
World.content:
Australians are increasingly turning to electric cars, with the national EV fleet now at about 650,000 vehicles.

During the June quarter alone the country recorded its biggest-ever quarterly surge in electric vehicle sales.

Nearly one in every two new vehicles sold was either electric or hybrid, according to the Australian Automobile Association.

In the year-to-date, EVs make up 26.7 per cent of the total new vehicle sales market, more than double the 12 per cent share in the same period last year.

With the oil price shock earlier this year fuelling petrol prices, some motorists have been driven to EVs by the belief they have lower running costs.

EVs need annual servicing to run safely despite requiring less maintenance than traditional cars. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

But what about servicing and repairs? Is it actually cheaper to run an EV?

Here's what you need to know.

Do electric cars require servicing?

Yes, according to the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW).

Like any vehicle, an EV needs professional servicing and maintenance annually to run safely, according to its website.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

"EVs have fewer moving parts than petrol or diesel vehicles and require much less maintenance," the DCCEEW said.

"They typically only need to be professionally serviced, or inspected, annually."

The Electric Vehicle Council (EVC) shares the same view.

An EVC spokesperson said servicing was typically simpler and less frequent than for petrol or diesel-run cars.

"EVs don't need oil changes, spark plug replacements or many of the engine-related services associated with petrol or diesel cars," he said.

"Instead, servicing focuses on tyres, brakes, suspension, cabin filters, battery health checks, software updates and general safety inspections."

Do you want to share more about your experience with EVs? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me.

What are main areas that need maintenance?

Steering and suspension systems as well as tyres.

EV tyres are heavily constructed. (ABC News: Millie Roberts)

EVs are very heavy vehicles, with an average mid-size city car weighing 400 kilograms more than a traditional car, according to Clint Flower, an automotive teacher at TAFE NSW.

"Any component in the suspension system is working harder," Mr Flower said.

Clint Flower says battery filters are a car part exclusive to EVs and hybrid cars. (Supplied)

"The tyres are working harder, and they're special tyres. All the EV tyres, they're heavily constructed."

He said battery filters, that clean the air cooling the battery, were a component exclusive to EVs and hybrid cars.

"A lot of EVs are now running a battery filter, and the battery filter is just an additional part that might need changing," Mr Flower said.

" That offsets the lack of engine oil [when it comes to servicing]. "

What about costs?

According to fact sheets published by the New South Wales government, EV servicing costs are typically 40 per cent cheaper than servicing an equivalent internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle, depending on the vehicle and manufacturer.

EVs have far fewer moving parts than ICE vehicles, meaning fewer components that wear out or need replacement, the EVC says.

EVs typically have fewer moving parts than internal combustion engine cars. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

An EV has about 20 moving parts, while an ICE car can have more than 2,000.

"Drivers avoid costs associated with engine oil, fuel filters, exhaust systems, timing belts and many other traditional maintenance items," the council adds.

In summary, owning an EV could save an average of $3,000 per year based on lower charging costs compared to fuel and fewer parts, which means less maintenance, according to the EVC.

The latest analysis from Endgame Analytics, commissioned by the EVC, has found:

Driving an ICE vehicle with petrol at $2 per litre costs an average of $22.20 per 100km of driving, rising to $27.75 at $2.50 and $33.30 at $3 per litre

Battery-EV owners charging at 6pm, considered peak period, pay an average of $5.90 per 100km, dropping to $1.20 for midday charging.

What are common misconceptions about EVs?

Peter Jones from the Motor Trades Association of Australia (MTAA) said despite not having a traditional engine, EV owners still had to change oil.

Peter Jones says there is oil to change in EVs, even though they don't have an engine. (Supplied)

"In fact, most EVs have a transmission or reduction gearbox containing oil that must be changed on schedule," Mr Jones said.

"Some EVs use liquid coolant for the battery and inverter, which needs to be changed when required.

"And, like all cars, they have brake fluid that should be changed every two to three years, depending on the specification."

Another misconception is around battery life.

Mr Flower from TAFE NSW said the batteries were "very, very reliable".

"There's a lot of public fear that the batteries in a second-hand EV are going to fail shortly after purchase, and the cost of replacing that battery is going to outweigh the cost of the car," he said.

"A five-to-six-year cycle of an EV [is] only losing 4 or 5 per cent of its [battery] state of health from brand new.

" They're consistent with an internal combustion engine … [with the] same sort of deterioration curve. "

Clint Flower says EV batteries are "very reliable". (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Do we have enough EV technicians?

No, said Mr Jones. However, he explained more were being trained as demand increased.

Previous MTAA modelling forecast there would be about 8,400 EV technicians by 2028, rising to 13,000 by 2030.

Those wanting to qualify can complete a Certificate III in Automotive Electric Vehicle Technology, which trains technicians according to Australian standards and can be completed as an apprenticeship.

The EVC said the transition to electric vehicles created both a challenge and an opportunity for Australia's automotive workforce.

"We will need more technicians with EV qualifications as EV uptake grows, but the industry has time to prepare if training continues to expand," it said.

Despite 86,300 motor mechanics employed nationwide the occupation is experiencing shortages, according to the National Mining and Automotive Skills Alliance's 2026 Workforce Insights Report.

When asked whether traditional motor mechanics would be put off by EVs, Mr Flower said he believed most of them would adapt and learn.

World.title: How AI could help reduce your time waiting at a red light
World.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) already has a foothold in many industries across Australia, but it could soon help speed up your commute.

Currently, when you pull up at an intersection, your car is detected by loops under the road surface, and the traffic lights cycle through phases before turning green.

In Australia, this phase-based system has been commonplace since the 1950s, and while reliable, researchers say it may no longer be optimal.

The intersection of Queen and Edward Streets in Brisbane's CBD in 1940. (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

It may be the latest "buzzword", but Queensland University of Technology Professor Ashish Bhaskar says AI could help improve our understanding of the movement of traffic at an intersection and use that information to reduce delays.

In an Australian first, a Queensland council is set to trial the technology at a single intersection later this year.

Professor Bhaskar says cameras have the potential to improve visibility at an intersection and AI can leverage that "smartness" to provide a better input to the algorithm, leading to better traffic control.

That means the system will have greater awareness of the mix of cars, buses, pedestrians and cyclists at an intersection, and will act accordingly.

"Now you have more knowledge, you have more visibility of what is happening at the intersection," he says.

"Instead of focusing on being reactive to what's happening, you can be more proactive, looking at the network-wide level or the corridor level and then make decisions at different intersections."

Currently, loops under the road surface detect cars at an intersection. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

Unlike the phase-based system, the new technology does not run on a fixed cycle, with the combinations instead determined based on demand.

Professor Bhaskar says the algorithm can be fine-tuned to suit the area's needs, for example, to prioritise pedestrians in the CBD or cars in high traffic areas.

The $170,000 trial at Petrie in Queensland's Moreton Bay will start later this year and is expected to run until early 2029, with a low-traffic intersection isolated from the main transport network deliberately chosen.

The intersection of Moreton Parade and Paper Avenue at Petrie where next-generation traffic lights will be trialled later this year. (Supplied: City of Moreton Bay)

The City of Moreton Bay says a camera will identify objects, which will be fed back, before the controller and AI determine the best sequence based on the detection and algorithm.

The council says an evaluation of the intersection before and after the trial will help determine its success.

The system, by Austrian-based company SWARCO, is already operating in Denmark and in cities across Europe, and the company says councils across Australia have expressed interest.

In the US city of Pittsburgh, the AI-based system SURTRAC, by researchers from Carnegie Mellon University, was found in 2019 to have reduced the average travel time by 25 per cent, with cars spending up to 40 per cent less time idling.

The City of Moreton Bay says a camera will identify objects before the controller and AI determine the best sequence based on the detection and algorithm. (ABC News: Claudia Williams)

Looking beyond a single intersection

University of Sydney transport engineering associate professor Mohsen Ramezani has welcomed the move in Moreton Bay, but with caution.

He says he does not expect massive gains to be made at an individual intersection, with the "real challenge" being effectively managing traffic at closely spaced intersections in CBD's.

While he admits he might sound pessimistic, he supports councils taking on trials and being "open-minded" to how to manage transport.

He says if AI or a new approach could help, it would be a "game changer".

According to Dr Ramezani, the biggest area for improvement is in the algorithm rather than detection.

"We can equip an intersection with heaps of sensors," he says. "But it's the decision-making … that's the smartness that still needs to be improved."

Fines withdrawn as AI road safety camera controversy continues More than $1 million worth of fines issued as a result of AI-assisted road safety cameras in WA have been withdrawn in the six months since they were introduced.

Later this year, a two-year $15 million trial will begin in Brisbane.

Councillor Ryan Murphy says it will go beyond "making one intersection smarter" with AI to be introduced "into the traffic management system itself".

"By coordinating entire corridors, we can deliver more reliable journeys and keep Brisbane moving as our city continues to grow," he said.

The council says the project is in the final stages of procurement, with the roads to be part of the trial and further detail on how AI will be incorporated yet to be determined.

World.title: Family violence offenders must disclose new relationships under draft laws
World.content:
Serial family violence perpetrators in Tasmania could soon be listed on a public register, face six months in jail if they continue to offend, and need to tell police when they start a new relationship, under draft changes to the Family Violence Act 2004.

The changes are being proposed by the state government.

"The proposed new framework will be one of the most comprehensive in Australia and the world … it's nation-leading," Attorney-General Guy Barnett said.

" It sends a clear message to serial offenders that family violence will not be tolerated, and those who continue to cause harm will be held to account. "

It will be at a judge's discretion whether to add a name to the list and would take into account whether it would identify a victim of family violence.

"Ultimately, that's a decision for the judge," Mr Barnett said.

"But in short, if you have two indictable offences or three summary offences then the judge can make that declaration … and the declaration is in place for a minimum of two years or until the behaviour change programs are completed."

In Tasmania, there are currently more than 400 serial family violence offenders.

"Tasmanian magistrate courts saw a 40-per-cent increase in applications relating to a breach of a family violence order or police family violence order in 2024 to 25," Mr Barnett said.

" This is deeply concerning and demonstrates that there is a cohort of perpetrators who continue to disregard the safety of victim-survivors. "

Guy Barnett says the draft laws send a "clear message to serial offenders". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Other proposed changes include reviewing the threshold for declaring someone a serial family violence perpetrator, and requiring offenders to complete a mandatory behavioural change or rehabilitation program.

Only at the completion of the program can a serial family violence perpetrator declaration be lifted.

If no effort is made to engage in a behaviour change program, then the declaration will remain for a minimum of two years.

Bree Klerck from the Tasmanian Family and Sexual Violence Alliance said the behaviour change programs were vital.

Bree Klerck says serial domestic violence offenders are falling through the gaps. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"Serial offenders are a real problem. We're hearing that quite a lot from police as well and that's putting a lot of pressure on the system," she said.

"If we're not seeing those behaviour changes, then the opportunity to continue offending in other relationships is going to happen.

"At the moment, we're seeing a lot of offenders falling through the gaps, and women and children are still feeling unsafe. That is really important to make sure those measures are in place."

Concerns about high number of police family violence orders issued towards women On-the-spot family violence orders are designed to protect those impacted by domestic and family violence. But advocates say they can unfavourably backfire on victim-survivors.

A person's previous family violence convictions in another state or territory can be considered when determining whether someone is a serial family violence perpetrator under the changes.

Courts could also be given additional powers to impose conditions to prevent further family violence and protect current, former or potential partners.

Minister for Women and the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence Jo Palmer said, "we cannot see the continuation of the destruction that family violence is having on our communities".

" There must be consequences for this sort of behaviour. "

Jo Palmer says the actions of perpetrators impacts on the community. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

'Very long waitlist' for rehabilitation program

In Tasmania, a magistrate can make attending a rehabilitation program part of a family violence order.

The family violence offender intervention program has a waitlist of more than 200 people. It runs every 10 weeks and takes 12 participants each time.

In March, the wait time for the program was 18 to 24 months in the state's south, and six to nine months in the north and north-west.

Engender Equality chief executive Alina Thomas said the state also had a "very long waitlist" for support services.

Alina Thomas says there needs to be an equal investment in support services for victim-survivors. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

"We have about 200 people on our waitlist, so we need to make sure that while we're improving the criminal justice response, we're also making sure there's an equal investment in building up the resources for victim-survivors," she said.

" I would like to see alongside these reforms that we have a focus on victim survivor support services, especially access to non-government services. "

Ms Thomas also questioned whether having perpetrators listed on a public registry would impact the safety and privacy of victim-survivors.

Early intervention, more funding needed

Women's Legal Service Tasmania principal solicitor Zoe Craven said the reforms were only the tip of the iceberg of required changes.

"There needs to be a much longer process of consultation, especially with victim-survivor groups and the services that support and advocate for them," Ms Craven said.

"That [should] be followed by more extensive reforms that invest in early intervention, prevention and broader-scale system reform.

"More investment more broadly in education, health, housing: That's what is going to keep victim-survivors and their children safe.

Ms Craven said early intervention and systemic change were needed.

"You're not going to impact the levels of family violence that we're seeing simply by locking up offenders for longer or putting them on a register or making them report their new relationships," she said.

"We need to see that broader systems change and early intervention before victim-survivors and their children are safer."

The Tasmanian government said the draft legislation will be released by the end of the year for public consultation.

World.title: Security issues loom large over Prince Harry and Meghan's return to UK
World.content:
Prince Harry and his family's access to taxpayer-funded security is again in the spotlight after their plans to move back to the United Kingdom were revealed this week.

The issue has been a source of tension between the Duke of Sussex, Buckingham Palace and British authorities for several years.

Prince Harry, his wife Meghan and their two children are expected to relocate to England from the United States, where they have lived since 2020, before the end of this month.

It remains unclear whether a stalemate over their safety has been resolved.

On Thursday, local time, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the Sussexes' security arrangements were a "private matter".

"It's a matter for Harry and for Meghan, and we wish them well in the move that they are making," he said.

Prince Harry has previously styled the issue as a deal-breaker, and the family's decision to return to England came as a surprise.

Last year the duke told the BBC he "can't see a world" in which he would bring his family to the UK, due to safety concerns.

What's behind Harry and Meghan's UK return While a move to London now brings Meghan and Harry in closer proximity to the royal family, it does not solve the Windsor's complicated dynamics or the deep rift between two brothers.

The Sussexes were stripped of their publicly funded protection around the time they ceased to be working royals in early 2020.

Since then, an independent committee of public servants, police, and members of the royal household has assessed their eligibility for protection during rare visits to the UK on a case-by-case basis.

The duke launched an unsuccessful legal challenge over their decision to revoke his family's protection.

His request for royal protection during a visit to the UK last month was rejected.

Prince Harry and Meghan have been paying a private security team in California, and it is not clear whether they will join the royals when they relocate to Britain.

"I think what we can anticipate is that a threshold of security must have been reached that is satisfactory for Harry and Meghan and the children," royal commentator Afua Hagan told the ABC.

"If that hadn't been reached, this would not be happening. We don't know what the security arrangements are, we don't know where they're going to live, apart from we know there'll be a private residence outside of London."

Local media have reported the royal couple have enrolled their children Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, in UK schools.

Relationship with royal family remains strained

It is not clear why they have decided to return to England, although it has been suggested it could be to spend more time with King Charles III, who was diagnosed with cancer in 2024.

Prince Harry's relationship with his family has been strained for several years.

He and his wife gave an interview to Oprah Winfrey in 2021 in which they criticised the royal family and spoke about racism in the institution.

The duke's 2023 autobiography, which included claims of a physical altercation with his brother in 2019, is also believed to have burned several bridges.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has not travelled to the UK with her husband since Queen Elizabeth II's funeral in 2022. It's understood that the duke and his brother, Prince William, have not spoken since then.

Last year, Prince Harry and the king had a brief meeting at Clarence House which lasted less than an hour. There are conflicting accounts of how that went.

King Charles III is understood to be happy about the prospect of spending more time with his son's family. (Reuters: Carl Court)

It is understood King Charles III was made aware of the Sussexes' plans on Sunday, local time, and that he welcomed the opportunity to spend more time with them.

The ABC understands there are no plans for Prince Harry and Meghan to return to their roles as working royals.

Adding another complexion to the duke and his family's move is his strained relationship with the British press, which he accuses of racism and privacy breaches.

He and his wife have launched multiple legal cases against newspaper publishers in the country.

They have also kept their children's lives and faces largely away from cameras in Los Angeles, something that appears unlikely to happen when they return to the UK.

World.title: ‘Heinous’ crime: China’s disgraced property king sentenced to life in jail
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesCrime ‘Heinous’ crime: China’s disgraced property king sentenced to life in jail Bloomberg News August 21, 2026 — 6:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

China Evergrande Group’s founder Hui Ka Yan has been sentenced to life in prison, bringing an end to one of the most dramatic rise and fall stories in China’s corporate history. The disgraced property tycoon, once Asia’s second-richest man, had turned Evergrande into a poster child of corporate excess during China’s long real estate boom. But after his empire came crashing down following a 2021 default, he was caught in a dragnet of official investigations that ultimately caused his downfall. Hui Ka Yan was sentenced alongside 56 others involved in Evergrande, including his sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe. undefined/Xinhua via AP Hui, who appeared visibly aged in court with greying hair, was sentenced alongside 56 others involved in Evergrande, including his sons Xu Zhijian and Xu Tenghe. His assets will be confiscated, and his companies were fined a combined 15.82 billion yuan ($3.3 billion). The move draws a curtain on what for years was one of China’s great success stories. Hui had binged on debt during Evergrande’s expansion, turning it into the world’s most indebted developer as he transformed the property giant into a sprawling conglomerate.



But Chinese authorities concluded that his rise was built on deception. They said Hui had perpetrated a massive financial fraud that included inflating assets and concealing liabilities. Related Article Opinion

Inside China China’s property cancer is spreading through its economy Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist In 2017, Hui had a net worth of $US45.3 billion ($63.3 billiion), the highest in Asia, according to Forbes. By 2023, it had shrunk to an estimated $US3 billion. On Thursday, the court in Shenzhen ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. In April, Hui had pleaded guilty in a Chinese court to charges including illegally taking public deposits and fundraising fraud. “The amount involved in the crime is exceptionally large, the circumstances are particularly heinous, exceptionally heavy economic losses have been caused, and the harm to society is extremely grave,” a report from state media outlet Xinhua wrote, adding that Evergrande and Hui “must be severely punished in accordance with the law.”



Evergrande and Hui were also found guilty of fraudulently issuing securities, violating information disclosure rules as well as bribery. Meanwhile, the founder was accused of embezzling company assets through dividend mechanisms. The sentence doesn’t bring an end to the numerous legal fights surrounding Evergrande. The company is now in liquidation, with an army of creditors inside and outside of China poring over its assets in the hopes of recovering some of their heavy losses. During its prime, Evergrande built more than 1300 projects across 280 cities. Bloomberg Rags to riches Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin in Mandarin, was born in Henan province in 1958 and grew up in poverty. Encouraged by the prospect of Deng Xiaoping’s economic reform plan, the son of a wood cutter quit his job at a steel firm in 1992 and later began developing property in Guangzhou, the provincial capital of Guangdong. He then founded Evergrande in 1996 and rode the wave of China’s unprecedented real estate boom.



Evergrande, which means “permanence and greatness” in Chinese, relied on heavy borrowing to fuel its growth, becoming the largest dollar-debt borrower among its peers and for a time the country’s biggest developer by sales. During its prime, the firm built more than 1300 projects across 280 cities. Supercharged by real estate riches, it also expanded its reach into industries ranging from bottled water to professional soccer and electric vehicles. For a long time, Evergrande skirted liquidity scares by tapping tycoons in China and Hong Kong to buy the firm’s stock and bonds. Hui also turned to his own suppliers and retail investors for financial backing. But Beijing’s crackdown on the property sector since 2020 capped its borrowing capacity, effectively cutting Hui off from credit markets. Hui’s charges follow a long list of harsh actions by Chinese authorities against corporate magnates. The sentence doesn’t bring an end to the numerous legal fights surrounding Evergrande. The company is now in liquidation, with an army of creditors inside and outside of China poring over its assets in the hopes of recovering some of their heavy losses. Anbang Group’s former chairman, Wu Xiaohui, was sentenced to 18 years in prison for fraud and embezzlement in 2018. That same year, China Huarong Asset Management Co. Chairman Lai Xiaomin was arrested amid a corruption scandal before being executed in 2021 on charges including bribery. HNA Group chairman Chen Feng was detained a few months later along with chief executive officer Tan Xiangdong for unspecified crimes.



Evergrande defaulted on its debt in late 2021. Following failed restructuring attempts, it was given a winding up order in Hong Kong in 2024, marking a significant escalation in the unravelling of the sector. Later that year, a mainland Chinese court accepted a liquidation application filed against one of its major onshore units. Hui was taken away by Chinese police in 2023 and held under so-called residential surveillance — a type of police action that falls short of formal detention or arrest. Apart from a company filing confirming Hui being put under control, Chinese authorities had remained tight-lipped about his status since then. Related Article Opinion

Inside China The Chinese dream has turned into a nightmare In 2024, Chinese regulators accused Evergrande’s main onshore unit of inflating more than 560 billion yuan of revenue by recognising sales in advance, an alleged fraud that dwarfs that of Luckin Coffee and Enron. China then suspended the operations of PricewaterhouseCoopers, Evergrande’s long-time auditor, for six months and imposed fines. Much of Hui’s known wealth was derived from his controlling stake in Evergrande and the cash dividends he’s received from the company since its 2009 listing in Hong Kong. Hui had pocketed more than $US7 billion over the past decade, thanks to the firm’s generous payouts, according to Bloomberg calculations.



Bloomberg, Reuters The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: ASX set to slide, Wall Street declines as oil rises on escalating Middle East tensions
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to slide, Wall Street declines as oil rises on escalating Middle East tensions Stan Choe Updated August 21, 2026 — 6:12am ,first published 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A rise in oil prices is sending worries about inflation and yields in the bond market higher, erasing some of the relief the US Treasury Department created the day before. The higher yields and a big drop for Walmart helped drag the US stock market lower. The S&P 500 fell 0.9 per cent for its fourth loss in the five days since setting its record last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1 per cent. Treasury yields climbed after the price of Brent crude rose 2.4 per cent following President Donald Trump’s latest threat to Iran. Wall Street closed in the red for the fourth time in five days. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to decline, with futures at 4.55am AEST pointing to a fall of 23 points or 0.3 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.3 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.10¢. Guzman y Gomez and Inghams are among the companies scheduled to report earnings today. The bond market remains the centre of the action after yields charged higher through the summer on worries about high inflation, gargantuan government debts and other factors. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent made a move that jolted financial markets to at least double the size of his department’s planned purchases of longer-term Treasurys from September 9 through November 4.



That helped push yields down after the 10-year Treasury’s yield had hit its highest level in more than a year and the 30-year yield got back to where it was in 2007, before the Great Recession sent yields toward zero worldwide. It’s a big deal because high yields slow the economy by raising interest payments for people, companies and the government, and they can undercut prices for stocks and other investments. Related Article Opinion

GST The GST carve-up is cooked, but we need to stop piling onto WA Millie Muroi Economics Writer But analysts had cautioned the effect may be short lived, given how small the purchases are relative to the overall size of the Treasury market and how they don’t fix the fundamental concerns of investors that had driven up yields. Plus, more signals arrived quickly to push worries higher. The US government’s debt topped $US40 trillion ($56.2 trillion) on Wednesday, a staggering record that arrived just months after the national debt first blew past the $US39 trillion mark in April, because Washington continues to spend far more money than it brings in. And on Thursday, the price for a barrel of Brent crude climbed 2 per cent to $US93.41 as uncertainty continues about when the war with Iran will allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. President Donald Trump threatened Iran with “the MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY” late on Wednesday but provided few details.



That helped push the 10-year Treasury yield up to 4.70 per cent from 4.65 per cent late Wednesday. It’s almost back to its 4.71 per cent level from late Tuesday, before the Treasury Department made its announcement. A couple encouraging reports on the US economy also helped push up longer-term Treasury yields, which move with expectations for the economy and inflation in coming years. One said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week than economists expected, while another said manufacturing in the mid-Atlantic region appears to be much stronger than expected. On Wall Street, Walmart was one of the heaviest weights on the S&P 500 and fell 9.2 per cent even though it reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on how an important underlying measure of revenue growth at its stores slowed again. Its forecast for profit in the current quarter also fell short of analysts’ expectations. Given its massive size, Walmart offers a look at how shoppers are doing across the United States. A surprisingly weak update on sales at US retailers overall last month had raised worries that shoppers may be succumbing to pressure from high inflation and a job market that may be looking less solid. Advance Auto Parts tumbled 24.6 per cent after the retailer reported weaker revenue for the latest quarter, even though its profit topped expectations. CEO Shane O’Kelly said that “tighter household budgets constrained spending more than we anticipated, especially during the last four weeks of the quarter.”



Spending by US consumers is the main engine of the economy, and a pullback by them could exacerbate what’s already a slowdown in growth for the economy. A pullback could also mean a double-whammy for travel companies, which would see fewer bookings when they have to pay higher prices for fuel. Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings fell 3.4 per cent, while United Airlines sank 3.5 per cent and American Airlines lost 2.5 per cent. Related Article Analysis

Trump's America Trump’s America faces a ‘doom loop’ as it falls in a $56 trillion hole Helping to keep Wall Street’s losses in check was Deere, which reported stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It rose 6.9 per cent as the company said order trends indicate the agriculture equipment business looks set to accelerate after this year. Oil companies also rose with the gains for crude prices. Exxon Mobil added 0.8 per cent, and ConocoPhillips climbed 3.3 per cent.



In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following a stronger finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi soared 5.9 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves after the two tech titans that dominate its market, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, jumped. Such swings have become more common for Seoul’s market, which has borne the brunt of rising and falling worries that winning stocks in the artificial-intelligence boom may have shot too high.
